[Bug] 0.29 batcher emits reason="node added" for long-existing nodes, fanning a full netmap rebuild to every connected peer
body:
### Description

After upgrading from 0.28.0 to 0.29.3, the control plane's steady-state CPU roughly tripled and has kept climbing. The debug log shows the batcher emitting `reason="node added"` changes for nodes that have existed for months, at a rate roughly 8–14x the number of actual client connections. Each one appears to trigger a netmap rebuild fanned out to every connected peer.

At our node count this saturates the server: map delivery to the subnet routers no longer completes inside the 5s HA probe timeout, both routers are marked unresponsive, and the primary never fails over — so subnet routes black-hole.

### Environment

- headscale 0.29.3 (previously 0.28.0), official image
- SQLite, single replica
- 617 node records, ~130 online, ~115 with an active long-poll connection
- ~139 advertised subnet routes across two HA subnet routers
- policy v2, ACLs + `autoApprovers`

### What I observe

90 seconds of debug log, 6648 lines. Change reasons:

```
5721  reason="node added"
 696  reason="node online"
  13  reason="ping node"
   2  reason="policy change"
   2  reason="node offline"
```

Actual client connections in that same 90s — `poll.go > node added to batcher`:

```
6
```

`node online` reconciles exactly: 6 connections × 116 connected peers = 696. That path behaves as I'd expect.

`node added` does not. 5721 fan-out lines from `batcher.go:168`, across **115 distinct recipient node IDs** — i.e. every connected peer. The most-visible peer received **86** separate `node added` changes in those 90 seconds, against 6 real connections.

Sample lines:

```
DBG hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go:168 > node change processing started node.id=896 reason="node added"
DBG hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go:168 > node change processing started node.id=670 reason="node added"
```

Crucially, these fire for nodes that were not added. Three of the most frequent recipients:

| node.id | created |
|---|---|
| 420 | 2025-08-08 |
| 646 | 2026-02-07 |
| 955 | 2026-08-10 |

Node 420 has existed for a year and is still receiving `reason="node added"`. My reading is that a routine nodestore write — `last_seen`, endpoint refresh — is being classified as a node addition rather than an update, and takes the full-rebuild path instead of a cheap one.

### Cost

From `/metrics`, on a process ~190s old:

```
headscale_nodestore_nodes                                    617
headscale_nodestore_peers_calculation_duration_seconds_sum   189.1
headscale_nodestore_peers_calculation_duration_seconds_count 23
headscale_nodestore_snapshot_build_duration_seconds_sum      189.2
headscale_nodestore_snapshot_build_duration_seconds_count    23
headscale_nodestore_batch_size_sum                           468
headscale_nodestore_batch_size_count                         23
headscale_nodestore_queue_depth                              6
process_cpu_seconds_total                                    529.6
```

8.2s per peer calculation, snapshot build accounting for essentially all of it, queue depth never draining, and 529 CPU-seconds burned in 190s of wall time.

### Downstream failures

```
WRN send: connection failed error="connection 99: timeout sending to channel (likely stale connection)" conn.id=99 node.id=875
ERR failed to apply change error="sending map response to node 875: node 875: all connections failed, last error: connection 99: timeout sending to channel (likely stale connection)" node.id=875 reason="node added" worker.id=2
WRN HA probe: node did not respond node.id=955 timeout=5000
WRN HA probe: node did not respond node.id=646 timeout=5000
```

Both nodes failing the HA probe are the two HA subnet routers. They aren't down — the batcher can't reach them in time.

### When it started

Container CPU, 6-hour buckets, cores, across the upgrade:

```
Jul 26-31  nights 0.50-0.65   days 0.83-1.11     0.28.0
Aug 1-2    0.36-0.52                             weekend
Aug 3      0.37 -> 0.76 -> 1.10 -> 1.02          upgraded to 0.29.3
Aug 4      0.98  1.45  1.81  1.35
Aug 5      1.07  1.90  2.22  1.64
Aug 6      1.27  1.98  2.23  1.77
Aug 7      1.54  2.07  2.46  1.51
Aug 8-9    1.25-1.43 flat                        weekend
Aug 10     1.32 -> 2.25 -> 3.07
```

The overnight floor is the clearest signal: with almost nothing connected it was 0.50–0.65 before the upgrade and has never dropped below 1.25 since. Client count overnight didn't change, so this is per-change cost, not load. Nothing else changed on Aug 3.

### Expected

A `last_seen` or endpoint update on an existing node should not be classified as `node added`, and should not force a full snapshot rebuild fanned out to every connected peer.

### Notes

I saw #3293 (`0.29 beta triggers PolicyChange on every reconnect causing CPU spikes`) and this looks like a different path — our `policy change` count is 2 per 90s, so that fix is working. Happy to supply more log or metrics detail.

title: api/v2: expose current or last known confirmed IP
body:
I've ammended this PR to replace `otherKnownIPs` with the Tailscale-compatible device posture endpoint:

` GET /api/v2/device/{id}/attributes`

It exposes `ip:publicAddress`, containing the current or last known (likely public) address from which the device most recently made an authenticated connection to Headscale. The value is persisted so it remains available while the device is offline.

The address comes from Headscale’s web server connection information, not from the device’s reported Magicsock endpoints. Existing `trusted_proxies` configuration is respected when Headscale is behind a reverse proxy.

The endpoint returns empty attribute and expiry objects until an address has been observed. This change also adds the corresponding OAuth scopes, database migration, generated client support, and tests.

title: state,change,mapper: report LastSeen for online peers per tailcfg protocol
body:
tailcfg documents `Node.LastSeen` as "when the node was last online … nil if never been online", and `PeerChange.LastSeen` as accompanying online-status changes. headscale only sent `LastSeen` for offline peers and never included it in online/offline patches, so clients on the new InitialStatus + peer-delta code path (Tailscale 1.102 on Apple platforms, tailscale/tailscale@`6bf05cb63`) saw online peers as never-online — rendering exit nodes as offline in the GUI.

- emit `LastSeen` for online peers in `TailNode`, per tailcfg semantics
- set `LastSeen` on connect/disconnect in `State` and carry it in the `NodeOnline`/`NodeOffline` change patches

Covered by a new servertest regression test and updated change/mapper tests. Note: this alone does not fix the empty exit-node list from #3415 — that turned out to be the GUI requiring a suggested exit node; see the issue for analysis and a policy (`nodeAttrs`) workaround.

Updates #3415

title: [Bug] Ephemeral node deleted between successful registration and initial PollNetMap, bypassing inactivity_timeout
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

With `node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout: 30m` configured, an ephemeral node registers successfully and is then deleted within ~20 seconds — before the client's first netmap poll completes. The client then polls a node ID that no longer exists until `tailscale up` hits its 60s deadline and fails.

The deletion appears to be triggered by the registration connection closing. headscale logs `Deleting ephemeral node during logout` for nodes that are still `node.online=true`, and that path does not appear to honour `inactivity_timeout`.

### Client side

```
16:55:21.239  control: RegisterReq: onode= node=[UCaU8] fup=false nks=false
16:55:23.818  control: RegisterReq: got response; nodeKeyExpired=false, machineAuthorized=true
16:55:43.395  Received error: PollNetMap: initial fetch failed 500: internal server error
16:55:43.462  Received error: PollNetMap: initial fetch failed 404: node not found
16:55:43.566  Received error: PollNetMap: initial fetch failed 404: node not found
16:55:43.787  Received error: PollNetMap: initial fetch failed 404: node not found
16:55:44.112  Received error: PollNetMap: initial fetch failed 404: node not found
              ... 404 for the next 37s; the client never re-registers ...
16:56:21.022  Sending SIGTERM to tailscaled
16:56:21.022  failed to auth tailscale: tailscale up failed: context deadline exceeded
```

Note the node is authorised at `16:55:23.818` and is already gone by `16:55:43.395`.

### Server side, same failure class

```
ERR http internal server error error="node no longer exists in NodeStore: 112901" code=500
ERR ephemeral node deletion failed node.id=112873
ERR user msg: node not found code=404
INF Deleting ephemeral node during logout machine.key=[...] node.expired=false node.id=112894 node.is_tagged=false node.online=true user.name=actions
```

### Scale

A sustained **~1,800 `node not found code=404` per hour**, measured flat across six consecutive hours (~43,000/day):

```
05:00  1728        09:00  1840
06:00  1835        10:00  1998
07:00  1836
08:00  1890
```

At roughly 60 client retries per lost registration, that implies on the order of **700 failed registrations per day**. This affects both CI runners (correctly ephemeral, one node per job) and long-lived service nodes that share an ephemeral pre-auth key. Observed symptoms downstream include failed GitHub Actions steps and ECS tasks whose `tailscale up` sidecar exits non-zero, taking the workload with it.

### Three secondary defects in the same code path

1. The follow-up poll returns **500** (`node no longer exists in NodeStore: N`) rather than 404 — a lookup race surfaced to the client as a server error.
2. `ephemeral node deletion failed` logs **no error**, so the reason is discarded. Observed 4 times in a 3-minute window.
3. `ERR user msg: node not found code=404` carries **no node identifier**, which makes ~43,000 events a day unattributable to a node, user, or machine key.

### Expected Behavior

1. A node authorised by `RegisterReq` (`machineAuthorized=true`) should still exist when the client makes its immediately following `PollNetMap` request. Registration and the initial map poll are separate HTTP requests, so the node must survive the gap between them.

2. Ephemeral deletion triggered by a connection close should respect `node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout`. With `30m` configured, a node should not be deleted ~20 seconds after registration while still marked `node.online=true`.

3. A request for a node that does not exist should return **404**, not **500**. `node no longer exists in NodeStore` is a normal outcome of a race, not an internal error.

4. `ephemeral node deletion failed` should log the underlying error. At present the failure is recorded but the cause is discarded, so there is no way to tell whether the node was leaked.

5. `node not found` should log the node ID or machine key, so occurrences can be attributed.

### Steps To Reproduce

This is a race, so it is probabilistic rather than deterministic — but at roughly 700 occurrences a day it reproduces readily under churn.

1. headscale 0.29.3, policy mode `file`, with `node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout: 30m` set.

2. Create a reusable **ephemeral** pre-auth key with a tag:

   ```
   headscale preauthkeys create --user <user> --reusable --ephemeral \
     --tags tag:<tag> --expiration 8760h
   ```

3. Have an ACL that gives that tag visibility of a large peer set. In our case tagged nodes see ~300 peers, which makes the initial netmap fetch expensive — it measured **19.6s** in the trace above. The wider that window, the more often the race is lost.

4. Register ephemeral nodes repeatedly, a few tens per hour. Any of these will do:

   - the `tailscale/tailscale` container with `TS_AUTHKEY` set, `TS_USERSPACE=true`, and **no persisted `TS_STATE_DIR`**, so every start generates a new machine key
   - CI runners using the same key
   - `tailscale up --login-server <url> --authkey <key> --reset` in a loop, from a fresh state directory each time

5. Watch the control plane:

   ```
   journalctl -u headscale --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager \
     | grep -c 'node not found code=404'
   ```

   A steady rate appears immediately. A fraction of registrations lose the race outright, and those clients fail with `tailscale up failed: context deadline exceeded` after 60s without ever re-registering.

The frequency scales with how long the initial netmap fetch takes, so a larger peer set per node makes it more reproducible. Conversely, a small tailnet may hide it entirely.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (noble), arm64 — AWS Graviton3, m7g.2xlarge (8 vCPU), kernel 7.0.0-1010-aws
- Headscale version: 0.29.3 (.deb on systemd, not a container)
- Tailscale version: 1.102.2 (`v1.102.2-teb67e5dcb`); minimum enforced client 1.80.0
- Number of nodes: ~310

Headscale network shape:

Single headscale instance, SQLite, policy mode `file`. Around 70 tagged nodes and 240 user-owned. Three subnet routers, two split-DNS resolvers, and the embedded DERP server (region 999) enabled alongside Tailscale's default DERP map.

The nodes are **not** all interconnected. The ACL scopes user-owned nodes to tagged destinations plus `autogroup:self` and `autogroup:internet`, so a laptop sees ~74 peers while a tagged node sees ~300. That asymmetry matters here: the expensive initial netmap fetch is on the tagged side, and tagged nodes are the ones failing.

Churn is heavy — roughly 400 node registrations a day from CI runners and ECS tasks, all using a reusable ephemeral pre-auth key with no persisted state directory, so each start generates a new machine key.

Relevant non-default settings:


policy:
  mode: file
node:
  expiry: 30d
  ephemeral:
    inactivity_timeout: 30m


The process also runs with `GOGC=800` (set to reduce GC overhead — see the allocation figures in the debug section; the default made it worse, not better).
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

### Contributing factor: the initial netmap fetch is slow, which widens the race window

In the trace above the initial fetch took **19.6s** before erroring. For a tagged node it builds peers for ~300 nodes, and a CPU/heap profile of the running process shows almost all of that work is one function:

```
$ go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space -top -nodecount=12 heap.pprof
Showing nodes accounting for 30426.55GB, 98.50% of 30889.27GB total

      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
14129.39GB 45.74% 45.74% 14129.39GB 45.74%  go4.org/netipx.(*IPSetBuilder).AddRange
 5567.49GB 18.02% 63.77%  5637.27GB 18.25%  go4.org/netipx.mergeIPRanges
 4297.18GB 13.91% 77.68% 14131.31GB 45.75%  go4.org/netipx.(*IPSetBuilder).IPSet
 4196.86GB 13.59% 91.26%  9834.13GB 31.84%  go4.org/netipx.(*IPSetBuilder).normalize
   55.64GB  0.18% 97.90% 26520.70GB 85.86%  policy/v2.(*PolicyManager).ViaRoutesForPeer
   12.93GB 0.042% 98.38% 26540.27GB 85.92%  types.NodeView.TailNode
    0.15GB 0.00047% 98.50% 26577.11GB 86.04%  mapper.(*MapResponseBuilder).buildTailPeers
    0.10GB 0.00032% 98.50% 26874.81GB 87.00%  mapper.generateMapResponse
```

`ViaRoutesForPeer` accounts for **85.86% of all allocation** (26.5 TB of 30.9 TB) because it is called once **per peer per map response** and builds a fresh `netipx.IPSet` each time. The CPU profile agrees from the other side:

```
$ go tool pprof -top -nodecount=10 cpu.pprof
Duration: 30.02s, Total samples = 113.84s (379.24%)

      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
    17.51s 15.38% 15.38%     20.73s 18.21%  runtime.tryDeferToSpanScan
    15.10s 13.26% 28.65%     23.34s 20.50%  go4.org/netipx.mergeIPRanges.func1
     6.29s  5.53% 34.17%      9.33s  8.20%  net/netip.Addr.Compare
     3.15s  2.77% 41.16%     21.48s 18.87%  runtime.bulkBarrierPreWrite
     2.29s  2.01% 52.64%     30.72s 26.99%  sort.partition_func
     1.25s  1.07% 66.50%     58.44s 51.34%  go4.org/netipx.mergeIPRanges
```

`mergeIPRanges` is **51.34% of CPU** — the same IP ranges re-sorted thousands of times a second. Measured allocation rate is ~820 MB/s sustained, which drives 16 GC cycles/second at default `GOGC` (hence the `GOGC=800` above).

Steady-state metrics for context:

```
headscale_nodestore_snapshot_build_duration_seconds  mean 1.074s   p95 2.31s
headscale_nodestore_peers_calculation_duration_...   mean 1.074s
headscale_nodestore_queue_depth                      0
headscale_mapresponse_generated_total{peers}         ~38/s
headscale_mapresponse_generated_total{policy}        ~1.5/s
process_cpu_seconds_total                            ~1.4 cores sustained
```

I intend to file the `ViaRoutesForPeer` allocation behaviour as a separate performance issue and will cross-link it. It is relevant here only because a faster initial fetch would narrow the window this race needs.

### Also worth noting

`headscale_mapresponse_generated_total{response_type="policy"}` runs at ~1.5/s on a policy file that never changes. The ACL uses `autogroup:self`, which sets `grantCategorySelf` and makes `hasPerNodeGrants()` true, so the compiled filter set holds one entry per node — meaning ordinary node churn mutates it and fans out a policy update. That may be expected, but it was surprising.

title: Reject unknown OAuth client scopes at creation
body:
Fixes #3406

- [x] have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) file
- [x] raised a GitHub issue or discussed it on the projects chat beforehand (#3406)
- [x] added unit tests
- [ ] added integration tests — the behaviour is fully covered at the `db.CreateOAuthClient` chokepoint every caller (CLI and v2 API) goes through; happy to add an `integration/cli_oauth_clients_test.go` case if you'd prefer one.
- [ ] updated documentation if needed — the CLI `--scope` help text now also lists `users`, which was already part of the vocabulary
- [x] updated CHANGELOG.md

## Problem

`CreateOAuthClient` validated tags via `validateACLTags` but not scopes: any string was deduplicated, sorted and stored verbatim, so `headscale oauth-client create -s 'EVIL:superuser' -s '../../etc/passwd'` succeeded. Since an unknown scope satisfies nothing in `scope.Grants`, this silently mints a client with fewer permissions than the operator asked for, and a typo like `auth_key` fails at request time rather than creation time.

## Change

- `scope.Scope.Valid()` reports membership in the existing `scope.Known()` vocabulary — the canonical list already used by the grant predicate, so validation cannot drift from enforcement.
- `db.validateScopes` replaces the inline dedup/sort in `CreateOAuthClient`, rejecting unknown values with `ErrOAuthClientScopeInvalid` and an error naming the accepted set.
- `mapError` maps that error to 400, so an invalid scope surfaces exactly like an invalid tag does today.
- Validation lives in the db layer rather than the CLI so the v2 API path (`POST` keys) is covered too.

## Verification

```
go build ./...                       # clean
go vet ./...                         # clean
gofmt -l .                           # no output
go test ./hscontrol/... ./cmd/...
```

Test suite is clean apart from two failures that also reproduce on an unmodified checkout in this environment: `TestAPIv2OAuthScopes` (needs `tofu`, provided by the nix dev shell) and `TestDialHeadscaleSocketRetriesUntilPresent` (macOS unix socket path length).

title: feat(policy): support SSH session recording
body:
Closes #1793. Supersedes #1820, which was closed pending the policy rewrite — this is that same feature written against `policy/v2`.

## Why this is small

`tailscaled` has understood `tailcfg.SSHAction.Recorders` and `OnRecordingFailure` since **capability version 61 (2023-04-18)**: given a recorder address it connects and streams the session as an asciinema cast. Headscale simply never populated those fields, so the capability has been unreachable from a headscale-managed tailnet even though every client already ships it.

This adds the two fields Tailscale's ACL syntax already uses — `recorder` and `enforceRecorder` — resolves the aliases at SSH policy compile time, and sets them on the action.

```json
{
  "ssh": [{
    "action": "check",
    "src": ["group:admins"],
    "dst": ["tag:prod"],
    "users": ["root"],
    "recorder": ["tag:recorder"],
    "enforceRecorder": true
  }]
}
```

## Three points for reviewer attention

**Recorders are set for both `accept` and `check`.** For check the client fetches a fresh action from `HoldAndDelegate`, but `tailssh.recorders()` falls back to the policy-derived `action0` when the delegated action carries none. That fallback is why check mode records without the delegate endpoint needing to know anything about recording, and it keeps this change inside one package — `noise.go` and the delegate handler are untouched.

It also matters beyond patch size: `sshCheck` is the only action that disables port forwarding (`sshAccept` hardcodes all three to `true`), so check is the only mode where a recording is a faithful account of the session. There is a test pinning the fallback specifically, because an innocuous refactor could remove it silently.

**Recorders must resolve to individual nodes.** `ConnectToRecorder` walks the list in order inside an overall budget of ~30s, so a recorder alias expanded from a wide prefix becomes hundreds of dial targets that exhaust the budget before reaching a live one — a policy-authored delay on every session establishment and, under `enforceRecorder`, a policy-authored SSH outage. Prefixes wider than a single IP are rejected rather than expanded, with a cap as a backstop. (#1820 assumed `ExpandAlias` had already reduced these to single IPs; this checks rather than assumes.)

**`enforceRecorder` with no resolvable recorder is an error.** Compiling it to a rule with no recorders would silently produce unrecorded sessions — the one outcome an operator who set that flag does not want.

## Smaller decisions

- `SSHAction.Message` carries a recording notice, adopted from #1820 — **credit to @Qup42**. Notice of monitoring is a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and the right default for a feature that exists to make sessions auditable.
- `OnRecordingFailure.NotifyURL` is deliberately left empty. It posts an `SSHEventNotifyRequest` back to control over the Noise transport and headscale implements no such endpoint; wiring one is a larger change and is not needed for recording to work. Happy to follow up separately if wanted.
- The recorder port is hardcoded to 80, matching Tailscale SaaS — the ACL syntax has no port field for recorders.

## Testing

```json
"action": {
  "holdAndDelegate": "http://headscale:8080/machine/ssh/action/...",
  "recorders": ["100.64.0.1:80", "[fd7a:115c:a1e0::1]:80"]
}
```

title: Fix inverted HTTP metrics skip condition
body:
### Problem

The `Skip` function passed to `metrics.Collector` in both routers had the condition backwards:

```go
Skip: func(r *http.Request) bool {
    return r.Method != http.MethodOptions  // skips everything except OPTIONS
},
```

A `Skip` function that returns `true` tells the middleware to **not** record metrics for that request. With `!=`, the function returns `true` for every method that is not OPTIONS — meaning GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and all other real traffic is silently excluded from `http_requests_total` and `http_request_duration_seconds`. Only `OPTIONS` preflight requests were ever counted.

### Fix

Change `!=` to `==` so OPTIONS (a CORS preflight with no application value in metrics) is the one method skipped, and all other traffic is recorded as intended.

The same inverted condition existed in both the main router (`createRouter` in `app.go`) and the Noise upgrade router (`NoiseUpgradeHandler` in `noise.go`). Both are fixed in this commit.

### Verification

```bash
# send regular requests to any endpoint
for i in $(seq 1 5); do curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health >/dev/null; done

# metrics now show http_requests_total with method="GET"
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9090/metrics | grep http_requests_total
```

Fixes #3412

title: hscontrol: allow changing a user's display name, email and profile picture
body:
Fixes #2166. Design document posted on the issue as required by CONTRIBUTING.md:
https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/issues/2166#issuecomment-5320904646

## What is missing today

`DisplayName`, `Email` and `ProfilePicURL` already exist end to end — the DB
carries them, `User.TailscaleUserProfile()` fills them, the mapper emits them,
and `headscale users create` accepts all three. The only gap is that they cannot
be changed afterwards: an operator who created a user before deciding on an
avatar has to destroy and recreate it, which is impossible once that user owns
nodes.

## What this adds

**`PUT /api/v1/user/{id}`** with pointer semantics: an absent field is left
alone, a present field is set — including the empty string, which clears it.
Clearing an avatar is a real operation, and GORM's struct-based `Updates()`
silently skips zero values, so the DB layer builds an explicit column map
instead. An empty body is a `400`, not a silent no-op.

`pictureUrl` is validated to be an absolute `http`/`https` URL, server-side and
in the CLI. This value is handed to every client's UI, so `javascript:` and bare
strings are rejected. (This also replaces the existing `url.Parse` check in
`users create`, which accepted almost anything.)

**`headscale users set`**, following the flag style of `rename`/`destroy`:

```console
$ headscale users set -i 1 --display-name "Vika" --picture-url "https://example.com/vika.png"
$ headscale users set -n vika --picture-url ""   # clear
```

`Flags().Changed` is what distinguishes "not passed" from "passed empty".

**OIDC users are refused**, reusing `ErrCannotChangeOIDCUser` exactly as
`RenameUser` already does. `User.FromClaim` rewrites all three fields on every
login — including to `""` when a claim is absent — so a manual edit would be
silently reverted. The provider stays the source of truth.

## Two bugs this surfaced

Both predate this feature and affect `RenameUser` and OIDC re-login as well: any
user mutation was invisible to already-connected nodes until a restart.

1. **Stale `NodeStore`.** `types.Node` embeds the owner and the mapper reads it
   from the snapshot via `NodeView.Owner()`, not from the DB. `UpdateUser` wrote
   the row and left the cached copies alone — there is an explicit
   `TODO(kradalby): We might want to update nodestore with the user data` at the
   site. Now every node of that user is re-pointed at the updated record in a
   single `NodeStore.UpdateNodes` batch.
2. **No map update was emitted.** `UpdateUser` returned only the policy
   manager's change, which is empty when the policy does not reference the user.
   It now returns `change.UserAdded()` — but *only* when a client-visible field
   actually changed, because OIDC calls `UpdateUser` on every login and
   broadcasting a full update to every node on every login would be a serious
   regression.

## Relationship to #3107

#3107 asks for the same capability but is written against the gRPC/protobuf
stack that was removed in #3324; the API is now code-first with huma and the Go
client is generated from OpenAPI via `make client`. This is a fresh
implementation against the current architecture rather than a rebase, and it
also covers the NodeStore/broadcast defects above. Happy to defer if @Razano26
would rather bring theirs forward instead.

## Tests

- `hscontrol/db/users_test.go` — set each field, clear with `""`, leave absent
  fields untouched, reject OIDC users and unknown ids, reject invalid URLs
- `hscontrol/state/user_profile_test.go` — the cached `Owner()` in the NodeStore
  reflects the new values, no broadcast on a no-op, rename covered too
- `hscontrol/types/users_test.go` — `ProfilePicURL` in all three tailcfg shapes
- `hscontrol/apiv1_users_test.go` — golden parity plus 400/404/OIDC guards
- `cmd/headscale/cli/users_test.go` — flag semantics
- `integration/cli_users_test.go` — `TestUserSetCommand`, registered in
  `test-integration.yaml`

Verdicts on this machine:

```
go test -race ./hscontrol/types/... ./hscontrol/db/... ./hscontrol/state/... ./hscontrol/api/...   ok
go test -race ./hscontrol/ -run TestAPIV1                                                          ok
go test ./cmd/headscale/cli/ -run TestSetUserRequestFromFlags                                      ok
golangci-lint run (v2.12.2, the version pinned in flake.nix)                                       0 issues
```

Each of the four commits builds and passes `go vet` on its own. Disabling the
NodeStore refresh makes `TestSetUserProfilePropagatesToNodeStore` and
`TestRenameUserPropagatesToNodeStore` fail, so they are real regression guards.

**Caveat:** the integration suite does not run locally here —
`Dockerfile.tailscale-HEAD` fails to build tailscale from source. I confirmed
this is environmental by running the pre-existing, unmodified
`TestUserCreateCommand`, which fails identically. `TestUserSetCommand` is written
but needs CI to validate.

## Verified end to end

Built this branch, ran it against a real `tailscale` client, and read the profile
the client received from the control server:

```
 id 1 | alice@example.com | DisplayName: Alice Rossi | ProfilePicURL: https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/9784476?v=4
```

Changing another user's picture propagated to that already-connected client
without a restart (confirming fix 2), clearing it returned the field to empty,
and `javascript:alert(1)` was rejected:

```
Error: profile picture URL must be an absolute http or https URL: "javascript:alert(1)"
```

## Maintenance

Three string columns and one endpoint, no external dependency and no background
work. The risk area is the NodeStore refresh in `UpdateUser`, which the state
tests cover. I am happy to maintain this.

title: serveLongPoll: "node has connected" log fires before mapBatcher.AddNode() registers the session, allowing a superseded session's reconnect-grace disconnect to clobber a fresh connect
body:
**Version:** v0.28.0 (also checked CHANGELOG.md through unreleased main/0.30.0 — no fix for this symptom landed as of 2026-08-18).

**Summary:** `hscontrol/poll.go`'s `serveLongPoll` already has a 10-second reconnect-grace debounce (checks `m.h.mapBatcher.IsConnected(m.node.ID)` before declaring a session disconnected) intended to prevent exactly this class of race. But the "node has connected" info log (`m.infof(...)`) fires before `mapBatcher.AddNode()` actually registers the session — so if an old, superseded session's grace-timer tick lands in that gap, `IsConnected()` still reads `false` and the old session's `Disconnect()` legitimately fires, flipping the node's online bit false immediately after (same-second, per our journal) a fresh, valid connect. Nothing re-arms the flag afterward absent a further connect transition — a node in steady state with an open long-poll doesn't re-log "connected," so the wrong bit persists indefinitely with no self-heal, even while WireGuard data-plane traffic (rekeys via DERP) continues normally and is fully independent of the control-session state.

**Evidence:** full-day `journalctl -u headscale` for one node showed exactly 4 events in the affected window — connect (old session), an error on the old session ("client disconnected"), connect (new session), disconnect (old session) — the disconnect trailing the new connect by <1s, all at 1-second log resolution. Node's `Online` bit read `false` continuously for the following ~35 minutes while `Last seen` kept advancing and WireGuard traffic was live and growing, confirmed independently via both the client-side `tailscale status` view and headscale's own `nodes list` server-side listing. Recovered only via a fresh, clean reconnect (a new connect transition), not by any elapsed time or additional traffic.

**Suggested fix direction:** register the session with `mapBatcher.AddNode()` before emitting the "connected" info log (or otherwise make the grace-timer's `IsConnected` check and the connect-log emission atomic/ordered), so a superseded session's belated grace-timer disconnect can't race a fresh connect that hasn't yet registered.

**Scope note:** this is not a "no debounce, last-transition-wins" gap — the debounce exists and is correctly designed in general; this is a narrow ordering bug inside it. Environment: embedded tsnet clients against a self-hosted headscale; the stuck bit reproduces on fast disconnect/reconnect (e.g. a client process restart).

title: [Bug] GivenName is not resynced when a node re-registers with a changed hostname
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [X] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

`GivenName` is resynced from a changed client hostname on the **MapRequest** path, but not on the **register/reauth** path. Because the reauth path already overwrites `node.Hostinfo`, the later MapRequest never observes a hostinfo change, so the resync that exists never runs. The node keeps its old DNS label indefinitely.

`hscontrol/state/state.go`, `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` — the resync exists and is correctly guarded against clobbering an admin rename:

```go
if hostinfoChanged {
    currentNode.Hostinfo = req.Hostinfo
    if req.Hostinfo != nil && req.Hostinfo.Hostname != "" {
        // Preserve an admin-renamed GivenName: only auto-derive when the
        // current GivenName is still what SanitizeHostname of the old
        // Hostname would produce (possibly with a "-N" collision bump).
        autoDerived := isAutoDerivedGivenName(currentNode.GivenName, currentNode.Hostname)

        currentNode.Hostname = req.Hostinfo.Hostname
        if autoDerived {
            currentNode.GivenName = dnsname.SanitizeHostname(req.Hostinfo.Hostname)
        }
    }
    ...
```

`hscontrol/state/state.go`, `applyAuthNodeUpdate` — same field, no resync:

```go
updatedNodeView, ok := s.nodeStore.UpdateNode(params.ExistingNode.ID(), func(node *types.Node) {
    node.NodeKey = regData.NodeKey
    node.DiscoKey = regData.DiscoKey
    node.Hostname = params.Hostname          // <-- hostname updated

    node.Hostinfo = params.ValidHostinfo     // <-- hostinfo updated too
    ...
    // GivenName is never considered
})
```

The second assignment is what makes this permanent rather than merely delayed. `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` computes `hostinfoChanged` by comparing the incoming `Hostinfo` against the stored one. Reauth has already stored the new `Hostinfo`, so the first MapRequest after reauth sees no change, takes the early-return branch, and the `autoDerived` block is never reached.

Net effect: `node.Hostname` and `node.GivenName` diverge permanently for any node that re-registers under a new hostname. MagicDNS keeps serving the old label (`GetFQDN()` uses `GivenName`), so the name a device answers to and the name it reports are different, with no warning surfaced anywhere.

This is self-latching. Once the two fields diverge, `isAutoDerivedGivenName(GivenName, Hostname)` returns false forever, so even a subsequent genuine MapRequest hostname change will no longer resync. The anti-clobber guard cannot distinguish "admin renamed this" from "reauth desynced this", and treats the desync as an intentional rename.

### Expected Behavior

`applyAuthNodeUpdate` applies the same `isAutoDerivedGivenName` guard that `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` already applies: when the stored `GivenName` is still auto-derived from the stored `Hostname`, re-derive it from the incoming hostname; when it has been admin-renamed, leave it alone.

Both paths mutate the same two fields for the same reason, so they should agree on the policy.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Register a node with hostname `host-a`. `Hostname` and `GivenName` are both `host-a`.
2. Change the client's hostname to `host-b` and re-register with an auth key (`tailscale up --force-reauth`, or logout/login). This is the normal path for automated (re)provisioning, where a device is re-imaged or renamed and re-enrolled with the same machine key and user.
3. `headscale nodes list` shows `Hostname=host-b`, `GivenName=host-a`.
4. `host-a.<base_domain>` still resolves; `host-b.<base_domain>` does not.
5. Wait for any number of MapRequests. The state never converges — step 2 already wrote the new `Hostinfo`, so `hostinfoChanged` is false from then on.

### Environment

```markdown
- Headscale version: v0.29.3 (also present on main @ 3390-line hscontrol/state/state.go)
- Tailscale version: multiple, 1.60-1.80
```

### Runtime environment

- [X] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Anything else?

**Proposed fix** — mirror the existing MapRequest logic in `applyAuthNodeUpdate`:

```go
updatedNodeView, ok := s.nodeStore.UpdateNode(params.ExistingNode.ID(), func(node *types.Node) {
    node.NodeKey = regData.NodeKey
    node.DiscoKey = regData.DiscoKey

    // Keep GivenName in sync with a client-side hostname change, using the
    // same rule as UpdateNodeFromMapRequest: only re-derive when the current
    // GivenName is still auto-derived, so an admin rename is preserved.
    if params.Hostname != "" && params.Hostname != node.Hostname {
        if isAutoDerivedGivenName(node.GivenName, node.Hostname) {
            node.GivenName = dnsname.SanitizeHostname(params.Hostname)
            // NodeStore.UpdateNode auto-bumps GivenName on collision.
        }
    }

    node.Hostname = params.Hostname
    ...
```

`NodeStore.UpdateNode` already bumps on collision via `resolveGivenName`, so the uniqueness constraint on `GivenName` is handled by the existing machinery.

**Note on existing deployments.** Nodes that have already desynced cannot be repaired by this fix alone, because the guard now reads them as admin-renamed. A detection helper would let operators find them:

```go
// Nodes where GivenName is neither auto-derived from the current Hostname
// nor from any plausible earlier one are indistinguishable from an admin
// rename, so surfacing them is the most that can be done automatically.
```

Two options that would each be useful on their own:

1. Extend the existing `hscontrol/state/node_health.go` checks with a `givenNameMatchesHostname` warning, alongside the current `givenNameMapsToValidFQDN`. Purely advisory, no behaviour change, and it makes the drift visible without an operator having to diff two columns by hand across the whole tailnet.
2. Add a `--reset-given-name` flag to `headscale nodes rename` (or a distinct subcommand) that re-derives `GivenName` from the current `Hostname`, so the repair does not require the operator to retype a name that headscale already knows.

Happy to open a PR for the `applyAuthNodeUpdate` change plus a regression test asserting that reauth with a changed hostname updates `GivenName` when auto-derived and preserves it after an explicit rename. Let me know if the health-check or CLI additions are wanted in the same PR or separately.

title: Resync the GivenName DNS label when a node re-registers
body:
## What?

A node that re-registers under a new hostname keeps serving its old MagicDNS label forever: `GivenName` is resynced from the hostname on the **MapRequest** path, but not on the **register/re-auth** paths.

Closes #3432

## Why?

Both re-registration paths overwrite the node's hostname and hostinfo in one step, and neither touches `GivenName`:

- `applyAuthNodeUpdate` sets `node.Hostname = params.Hostname` and `node.Hostinfo = params.ValidHostinfo`;
- `HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey`'s in-place update does the same (and already carries a TODO asking for the map-request merge semantics).

The resync that exists in `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` is guarded by `hostinfoChanged` — but re-registration has already stored the new `Hostinfo`, so the first MapRequest afterwards compares equal, takes the early-return branch, and never reaches the `autoDerived` block. The divergence is self-latching: once `Hostname` and `GivenName` differ, `isAutoDerivedGivenName` returns false forever, so even the MapRequest path stops helping. `GetFQDN()` uses `GivenName`, so MagicDNS keeps answering the old name indefinitely.

## How?

Mirror `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest`'s GivenName handling on both register paths, inside the existing `NodeStore.UpdateNode` mutation (so the collision-bump logic in `UpdateNode` applies as it does elsewhere):

```go
givenNameAutoDerived := isAutoDerivedGivenName(node.GivenName, node.Hostname)
node.Hostname = <new hostname>
if givenNameAutoDerived && <new hostname> != "" {
    node.GivenName = dnsname.SanitizeHostname(<new hostname>)
}
```

The `isAutoDerivedGivenName(node.GivenName, node.Hostname)` check runs against the **old** hostname (before it is overwritten), exactly as the MapRequest block does, so an admin rename keeps winning on every path. The empty-hostname guard matches the MapRequest block's `Hostname != ""` condition (relevant for the pre-auth-key path, where a client can omit hostinfo entirely).

## Testing

`TestReauthResyncsGivenName` (new, `hscontrol/state`), covering both paths and the rename guard:

- a node registered as `old-host`, re-registered via `HandleNodeFromAuthPath` as `new-host`: `GivenName` becomes `new-host`;
- an admin `SetGivenName("custom-label")` survives both a subsequent re-auth **and** a pre-auth-key re-registration under yet another hostname;
- a second node with an auto-derived label, re-registered via `HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey` as `pak-host`: `GivenName` becomes `pak-host`.

**Differential**: on the previous code the test fails with `#3432: GivenName must follow the new hostname when re-registering via re-auth`. Full `go test ./hscontrol/state/` (56s, the whole package) passes.

title: oidc: add oidcgrp: principal type for OIDC group-based ACLs
body:
## Summary

This PR adds OIDC group support to Headscale ACLs via the standard Tailscale-compatible
`group:<name>` principal. OIDC groups from any provider (Keycloak, Authentik, Zitadel,
Entra ID, etc.) are merged with policy-defined local groups under the same `group:<name>`
syntax, preserving the internal distinction between local and OIDC membership.

**Tests: All unit tests pass (4.4s) | go vet clean | gofmt clean | build clean**

---

## What Changed

### Core Changes (`hscontrol/`)

| Area | Files | Description |
|------|-------|-------------|
| **Data Model** | `types/users.go` | `UserOIDCGroup` model with composite unique index on `(user_id, group_name)` |
| **DB Migration** | `db/db.go` | Migration creating `user_oidc_groups` join table |
| **DB Layer** | `db/users.go` | `SetUserOIDCGroups` (Unscoped delete), `GetUserOIDCGroups`, `GetUsersByOIDCGroup` |
| **OIDC Login** | `oidc.go` | Store groups from `claims.Groups` after user creation/update |
| **Policy Engine** | `policy/v2/types.go` | `Group.resolve()` combines local + OIDC; `oidcgrp:` removed from `parseAlias()` |
| **Policy Engine** | `policy/v2/policy.go` | `SetOIDCGroupResolver()` on `PolicyManager` (preserved across reloads) |
| **Policy Manager** | `policy/pm.go` | Interface update for `SetOIDCGroupResolver` |
| **Group Refresh** | Background goroutine | `RefreshAllOIDCGroups()` clears stale memberships on 15-min interval |
| **Admin API** | API endpoints | `GET/PUT /api/v1/user/{id}/oidc-groups`, `GET /api/v1/user/oidc-group?group=` |
| **State** | `state/state.go` | Wiring for `SetUserOIDCGroups` → policy manager update |
| **Docs** | `docs/ref/oidc-groups.md` | Full documentation with `group:` syntax, examples, API reference |

### Removed

| Component | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| `e2e/` directory | Not part of headscale's integration test framework (per `integration/README.md` and maintainer feedback) |
| `oidcgrp:` public syntax | Not Tailscale-compatible; replaced by `group:<name>` |

---

## Architecture

```
OIDC provider
    |
    v
persistent OIDC memberships (user_oidc_groups table)
    |
    v
group resolution layer (Group.resolve())
    |
    +---- local Headscale group membership (policy groups section)
    +---- OIDC group membership (user_oidc_groups table)
    |
    v
group:<name>  (unified Tailscale-compatible principal)
    |
    v
policy resolver → nodes
```

### How `group:<name>` Resolves

1. **Local resolution**: Look up `p.Groups[groupName]` — returns `[]Username` from the
   policy's `groups` section. Each `Username` is resolved to user ID → nodes.

2. **OIDC resolution**: Call `oidcGroupResolver.GetUsersByOIDCGroup(groupName)` — returns
   `[]types.User` from the `user_oidc_groups` table. Each user is matched to their nodes.

3. **Deduplication**: Before adding OIDC users, collect user IDs already resolved from
   local groups. Skip any OIDC user whose ID appears in this set.

4. **Result**: A single `netipx.IPSet` containing all unique node IPs from both sources.

### Same-Group Name Conflict Resolution

| Scenario | Local | OIDC | Result |
|----------|-------|------|--------|
| Different users, same group | bob → engineering | alice → engineering | {bob, alice} |
| Same user in both sources | bob → engineering | bob → engineering | {bob} (deduplicated) |
| Group in only one source | bob → local-team | — | {bob} |
| Group in neither source | — | — | {} (empty set) |
| OIDC refresh | bob (local, unchanged) | alice removed | {bob} only |

**Key invariant**: The policy's `groups` section is never modified by OIDC refresh.
The `user_oidc_groups` table is never modified by local group changes.

---

## Policy Syntax

```json
{
  "groups": {
    "group:local-team": ["bob@headscale.local"]
  },
  "acls": [
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:engineering"],
      "dst": ["group:admins:443"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:engineering"],
      "dst": ["*:22"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:admins"],
      "dst": ["*:*"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:engineering", "group:local-team", "tag:server"],
      "dst": ["*:80,443"]
    }
  ]
}
```

- `group:engineering` resolves through **both** OIDC and local sources
- `group:local-team` is defined only locally (in the `groups` section)
- `tag:server` is a standard Tailscale tag
- `oidcgrp:` is **rejected** at parse time (not Tailscale-compatible)

---

## Internal Distinction Between Sources

| Source | Storage | Mutated by OIDC refresh? | Mutated by local changes? |
|--------|---------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| Local groups | Policy `groups` section (in-memory) | No | Yes (policy reload) |
| OIDC groups | `user_oidc_groups` DB table | Yes (login/periodic refresh) | No |

Both sources remain **separate** internally while exposing a unified `group:<name>`
principal externally. This ensures:
- OIDC refresh never removes local group memberships
- Local group changes never remove OIDC memberships
- Each source is independently auditable

---

## Preserved Code

| Component | Status |
|-----------|--------|
| `UserOIDCGroup` model + `user_oidc_groups` table | ✅ Preserved |
| `SetUserOIDCGroups()` / `GetUsersByOIDCGroup()` DB methods | ✅ Preserved |
| OIDC callback stores groups from `groups` claim | ✅ Preserved |
| `OIDCGroupResolver` interface (internal) | ✅ Preserved |
| `SetOIDCGroupResolver()` on `PolicyManager` | ✅ Preserved |
| Periodic OIDC group refresh | ✅ Preserved |
| Admin API endpoints | ✅ Preserved |
| DB migration | ✅ Preserved |

---

## Key Design Decisions

### Why `group:<name>` Instead of `oidcgrp:`?

Tailscale uses `group:<name>` as the standard policy principal. Adding `oidcgrp:`
creates a non-standard extension that breaks policy portability between Tailscale SaaS
and self-hosted Headscale. By merging OIDC groups into the existing `group:` resolution,
policies remain fully Tailscale-compatible.

### Why Not Silently Merge Sources?

The maintainer feedback explicitly states: "Do not silently destroy the distinction
between local Headscale membership and OIDC membership internally." The implementation
preserves both sources separately while exposing them through a unified `group:<name>`
principal. This ensures:
- OIDC refresh only modifies OIDC memberships
- Local group management only modifies local memberships
- Both sources are independently auditable and debuggable

### Why Relaxed Validation?

Groups referenced in policies may come from OIDC (not defined in the policy's `groups`
section). Strict validation at policy load time would reject valid OIDC-only groups.
Instead, undefined groups resolve to an empty set at evaluation time.

### Why `Unscoped()` Delete?

The `SetUserOIDCGroups` function uses `tx.Unscoped().Where(...).Delete()` instead of
a normal GORM delete. This is because:
- GORM uses soft deletes by default (sets `deleted_at` timestamp)
- The composite unique index `(user_id, group_name)` prevents re-inserting the same rows
- `Unscoped()` performs a hard delete, allowing re-insertion

---

## Testing

### Unit Tests (10 in oidcgrp_test.go)

| Test | What It Verifies |
|------|------------------|
| `TestGroupResolveFromOIDC` | OIDC-only group resolves via `group:` |
| `TestGroupResolveFromLocalPolicy` | Local-only group resolves via `group:` |
| `TestGroupResolveFromBothSources` | Both sources contribute to same `group:` |
| `TestGroupDeduplication` | User in both sources appears once |
| `TestGroupResolveEmptyOIDCGroup` | Empty OIDC group resolves to nothing |
| `TestGroupResolveNoResolver` | Graceful fallback when no OIDC configured |
| `TestSetOIDCGroupResolver` | Resolver injection triggers recompilation |
| `TestIsOIDCGroup` | Internal helper still works |
| `TestOIDCGroupNotInParseAlias` | `oidcgrp:` rejected from public syntax |
| `TestGroupResolveOIDCOnlyVsLocalOnly` | Different groups from different sources |

### Modified Tests (6 in types_test.go)

Groups not defined in the policy may now be OIDC-provided. Tests updated from
"group must be defined in policy" to "group may be OIDC-only."

### Verification

```
go vet ./hscontrol/policy/...     ✅ Clean
gofmt -l ...                      ✅ No issues
go build ./...                    ✅ Compiles
go test ./hscontrol/policy/v2/    ✅ All pass (4.4s)
```

---

## Security Considerations

1. **Stale OIDC memberships**: Periodic refresh clears old memberships. New memberships
   are populated on next login.

2. **Accidental privilege retention**: Removing a user from an OIDC group removes their
   OIDC-derived authorization after the next refresh/login.

3. **Local group isolation**: OIDC refresh never modifies the policy's `groups` section.
   Local group changes never modify the `user_oidc_groups` table.

4. **Concurrency**: The `PolicyManager` uses `sync.RWMutex` for concurrent access. The
   `oidcGroupResolver` is set once at startup and preserved across policy reloads.

5. **Empty OIDC provider response**: If the OIDC provider returns no groups, only local
   group memberships apply. No crash or error.

---

## Upstream Compatibility

- ✅ `group:<name>` is the standard Tailscale policy syntax
- ✅ `oidcgrp:` is rejected at parse time
- ✅ Policies are portable between Tailscale SaaS and self-hosted Headscale
- ✅ Follows existing Headscale architecture patterns
- ✅ No new custom principal syntax introduced

---

## Future Work

1. **Integration tests** — migrate useful scenarios into the project's `integration/`
   framework (per `integration/README.md`)
2. **Keycloak OIDC login flow** — test actual OIDC authentication end-to-end
3. **Race condition tests** — concurrent group writes + reads under load
4. **CI integration** — add integration tests to GitHub Actions

body:
We're self-hosting Headscale as a privacy-motivated alternative to the proprietary Tailscale coordination server, using the official Tailscale apps against our own server.

We initially evaluated NetBird as an alternative as well, but hit an (apparently known, unresolved) upstream bug where the iOS client completes the WireGuard handshake but never actually passes data through the tunnel (control plane fine, data plane empty). Switching the very same setup over to a self-hosted Headscale server instead fixed that completely — SSH connectivity from iOS worked flawlessly, no reconfiguration needed on our side beyond pointing the client at our Headscale URL. We were genuinely happy with the result.

Unfortunately, we then had to revert back to the original proprietary tailscale.com control server anyway, because we depend on **Tailscale Funnel** for exposing a self-hosted service (Home Assistant) to the public internet with a valid TLS certificate, and Headscale does not support Funnel (we found the older related discussion in #1040, which is closed).

Could Funnel support be reconsidered/prioritized? For us it's the single remaining blocker preventing a full switch away from the proprietary control server — everything else (basic connectivity, SSH, DERP, ACLs) has worked well in our testing.

Happy to help test if there's ever a branch/experimental build with partial Funnel support.

title: [Feature] # Discussion: OIDC Group Support via `group:<name>` — Tailscale-Compatible ACL Integration
body:
### Use case

**Related Issues:** #2366  
**Related PRs:** #3434 (original `oidcgrp:` implementation), existing upstream OIDC groups PR  

---

## Problem Statement

Headscale needs to support OIDC provider group memberships in ACL policies, but the
initial implementation introduced a custom `oidcgrp:<name>` principal type that is
**not Tailscale-compatible**. Tailscale's policy syntax uses `group:<name>` for
group-based ACLs. Adding a new principal type creates fragmentation and breaks
compatibility with Tailscale policy files.

### The Core Conflict

The same group name (e.g., `engineering`) can exist in **two separate systems**:

1. **Headscale-local groups** — defined in the policy file's `groups` section
2. **OIDC-provider groups** — fetched from the OIDC provider's `groups` claim

```json
// Local definition
{
  "groups": {
    "group:engineering": ["bob@headscale.local"]
  }
}

// OIDC definition (from provider)
// alice -> engineering (from OIDC groups claim)
```

Both must resolve through the **same** `group:<name>` principal in policy rules:

```json
{
  "acls": [{
    "action": "accept",
    "src": ["group:engineering"],
    "dst": ["*:*"]
  }]
}
```

The engineering group should include **both** `bob` (local) **and** `alice` (OIDC)
without duplication or conflict.

---

## Proposed Architecture

```
OIDC provider
    |
    v
persistent OIDC memberships (user_oidc_groups table)
    |
    v
group resolution layer
    |
    +---- local Headscale group membership (policy groups section)
    +---- OIDC group membership (user_oidc_groups table)
    |
    v
group:<name>  (unified Tailscale-compatible principal)
    |
    v
policy resolver
    |
    v
nodes
```

### Key Design Decision: Preserving Internal Distinction

The implementation **does NOT** silently merge local and OIDC groups into a single
internal model. The two sources remain separate:

| Source | Storage | Mutated by OIDC refresh? | Mutated by local changes? |
|--------|---------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| Local groups | Policy `groups` section (in-memory) | No | Yes (policy reload) |
| OIDC groups | `user_oidc_groups` DB table | Yes (login/periodic refresh) | No |

This separation ensures:
- OIDC refresh never removes local group memberships
- Local group changes never remove OIDC memberships
- Each source is independently auditable

---

## How Resolution Works

### `Group.resolve()` Method

The core resolution logic in `Group.resolve()` (types.go) works in two phases:

```go
func (g *Group) resolve(p *Policy, users types.Users, nodes views.Slice[types.NodeView]) (*netipx.IPSet, error) {
    var ips netipx.IPSetBuilder

    // Phase 1: Resolve local (policy-defined) group members.
    for _, username := range p.Groups[*g] {
        uips, err := username.resolve(nil, users, nodes)
        // ... add to ips
        ips.AddSet(uips)
    }

    // Phase 2: Resolve OIDC-provider group members.
    if p.oidcGroupResolver != nil {
        groupName := strings.TrimPrefix(string(*g), "group:")
        oidcUsers, err := p.oidcGroupResolver.GetUsersByOIDCGroup(groupName)
        if err == nil && len(oidcUsers) > 0 {
            // Deduplicate: skip users already resolved from local groups.
            localUserIDs := make(map[uint]bool)
            for _, username := range p.Groups[*g] {
                if user, err := username.resolveUser(users); err == nil {
                    localUserIDs[user.ID] = true
                }
            }

            for _, oidcUser := range oidcUsers {
                if localUserIDs[oidcUser.ID] {
                    continue // Already counted from local group.
                }
                // Find nodes owned by this OIDC user.
                for _, node := range nodes.All() {
                    if node.User().ID() == oidcUser.ID {
                        node.AppendToIPSet(&ips)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }

    return ips.IPSet(), nil
}
```

### Resolution Flow

1. **Local resolution**: Look up `p.Groups[groupName]` — returns `[]Username` from the policy's `groups` section. Each `Username` is resolved to user ID → nodes.

2. **OIDC resolution**: Call `oidcGroupResolver.GetUsersByOIDCGroup(groupName)` — returns `[]types.User` from the `user_oidc_groups` table. Each user is matched to their nodes.

3. **Deduplication**: Before adding OIDC users, collect user IDs already resolved from local groups. Skip any OIDC user whose ID appears in this set.

4. **Result**: A single `netipx.IPSet` containing all unique node IPs from both sources.

---

## Avoiding Same-Group Name Conflicts

### Scenario 1: Different Users, Same Group Name

```
Local:  bob -> engineering
OIDC:   alice -> engineering

group:engineering resolves to: {bob, alice}
```

**Behavior**: Both users are included. The IP set is the union of both users' nodes.

### Scenario 2: Same User in Both Sources

```
Local:  bob -> engineering
OIDC:   bob -> engineering

group:engineering resolves to: {bob} (counted once)
```

**Behavior**: The deduplication check in `Group.resolve()` detects that `bob`'s user ID
was already resolved from the local group and skips the duplicate. No double-counting
of IPs or filter rules.

### Scenario 3: Group Exists Only in One Source

```
Local:  bob -> local-team     (defined in policy groups)
OIDC:   alice -> oidc-team    (from OIDC provider, NOT in policy groups)

group:local-team  resolves to: {bob}     (local only)
group:oidc-team   resolves to: {alice}   (OIDC only)
```

**Behavior**: Both groups work correctly. A group not defined in the policy's `groups`
section resolves through OIDC only (and vice versa).

### Scenario 4: Group in Neither Source

```
group:nonexistent resolves to: {} (empty set)
```

**Behavior**: No users, no nodes, no filter rules. The ACL is a no-op.

### Scenario 5: OIDC Refresh Does Not Affect Local Groups

```
Before refresh:
  Local:  bob -> engineering
  OIDC:   alice -> engineering

OIDC refresh removes alice from engineering.

After refresh:
  Local:  bob -> engineering (unchanged)
  OIDC:   alice NOT in engineering

group:engineering resolves to: {bob} only
```

**Behavior**: The periodic OIDC refresh only modifies the `user_oidc_groups` table.
The policy's `groups` section is never touched. Bob's local membership is preserved.

---

## Policy Syntax Compatibility

### Before (Not Tailscale-Compatible)

```json
{
  "acls": [{
    "src": ["oidcgrp:engineering"],
    "dst": ["oidcgrp:admins:443"]
  }]
}
```

### After (Tailscale-Compatible)

```json
{
  "groups": {
    "group:local-team": ["bob@headscale.local"]
  },
  "acls": [{
    "src": ["group:engineering"],
    "dst": ["group:admins:443"]
  }]
}
```

The `group:` principal is the standard Tailscale syntax. OIDC groups resolve through
the same `group:` prefix, making policies portable between Tailscale SaaS and
self-hosted Headscale.

---

## Internal Model

### Preserved from Original Implementation

| Component | Status | Location |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| `UserOIDCGroup` model | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/types/` |
| `user_oidc_groups` DB table | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/db/` |
| `SetUserOIDCGroups()` | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/db/users.go` |
| `GetUsersByOIDCGroup()` | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/db/users.go` |
| `GetUserOIDCGroups()` | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/db/users.go` |
| OIDC callback group storage | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/oidc.go` |
| `OIDCGroupResolver` interface | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/policy/v2/types.go` |
| `SetOIDCGroupResolver()` | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go` |
| Periodic OIDC group refresh | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/state/state.go` |
| Admin API endpoints | ✅ Preserved | `hscontrol/apiv1/` |

### Changed

| Component | Before | After |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Public policy syntax | `oidcgrp:<name>` | `group:<name>` |
| `parseAlias()` | Accepted `oidcgrp:` | Rejects `oidcgrp:` |
| `Group.resolve()` | Local only | Local + OIDC |
| Policy validation | Required groups in policy | Allows undefined (may be OIDC) |
| Documentation | Used `oidcgrp:` syntax | Uses `group:` syntax |
| E2E tests | Used `oidcgrp:` | Uses `group:` |

### Removed

| Component | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| `oidcgrp:` public syntax | Not Tailscale-compatible |

---

## Security Considerations

1. **Stale OIDC memberships**: The periodic refresh clears old memberships. New
   memberships are populated on next login.

2. **Accidental privilege retention**: Removing a user from an OIDC group removes
   their OIDC-derived authorization after the next refresh/login.

3. **Local group isolation**: OIDC refresh never modifies the policy's `groups`
   section. Local group management never modifies the `user_oidc_groups` table.

4. **Concurrency**: The `PolicyManager` uses `sync.RWMutex` for concurrent access.
   The `oidcGroupResolver` is set once at startup and preserved across policy reloads.

5. **Empty OIDC provider response**: If the OIDC provider returns no groups, only
   local group memberships apply. No crash or error.

---

## Test Coverage

| Test | What It Verifies |
|------|------------------|
| `TestGroupResolveFromOIDC` | OIDC-only group resolves via `group:` |
| `TestGroupResolveFromLocalPolicy` | Local-only group resolves via `group:` |
| `TestGroupResolveFromBothSources` | Both sources contribute to same `group:` |
| `TestGroupDeduplication` | User in both sources appears once |
| `TestGroupResolveEmptyOIDCGroup` | Empty OIDC group resolves to nothing |
| `TestGroupResolveNoResolver` | Graceful fallback when no OIDC configured |
| `TestSetOIDCGroupResolver` | Resolver injection triggers recompilation |
| `TestOIDCGroupNotInParseAlias` | `oidcgrp:` rejected from public syntax |
| `TestGroupResolveOIDCOnlyVsLocalOnly` | Different groups from different sources |
| 6 modified existing tests | Groups may be OIDC-only (no validation error) |

---

## References

- Issue #2366: Supporting Group OIDC in ACLs
- Tailscale policy syntax: https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/syntax/policy-file
- Headscale contributing docs: https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
- Integration test docs: https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/main/integration/README.md


### Description

The old non-standard `oidcgrp:` principal was removed for Tailscale compatibility. ### How can it be implemented?

# How OIDC Groups Work in Headscale

## Overview

Headscale supports group-based ACL policies using the Tailscale-compatible
`group:<name>` principal. Groups can come from two sources:

1. **Local groups** — defined in the policy file's `groups` section
2. **OIDC groups** — fetched from the OIDC provider's `groups` claim

Both sources resolve through the same `group:<name>` syntax. The internal
distinction between sources is preserved.

---

## Two Sources, One Principal

### Local Groups

Defined in the policy file:

```json
{
  "groups": {
    "group:engineering": ["bob@headscale.local", "alice@headscale.local"]
  }
}
```

These are stored in-memory as `p.Groups[groupName] → []Username`.

### OIDC Groups

Fetched from the OIDC provider during login and stored in the database:

```sql
-- user_oidc_groups table
user_id | group_name
1       | engineering
2       | engineering
1       | platform
```

These are queried via `oidcGroupResolver.GetUsersByOIDCGroup(groupName) → []User`.

---

## Resolution Flow

When the policy resolver encounters `group:<name>`, it calls `Group.resolve()`:

```
group:engineering
        |
        v
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  Phase 1: Local Resolution    │
│                               │
│  p.Groups["group:engineering"]│
│  → [bob, alice]               │
│  → resolve each to node IPs   │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                |
                v
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  Phase 2: OIDC Resolution     │
│                               │
│  oidcGroupResolver            │
│  .GetUsersByOIDCGroup(        │
│    "engineering")             │
│  → [charlie] (from DB)        │
│  → resolve each to node IPs   │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                |
                v
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  Phase 3: Deduplication       │
│                               │
│  Collect user IDs from Phase1 │
│  Skip OIDC users already in   │
│  Phase1 set                   │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                |
                v
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  Result: Single IP Set        │
│                               │
│  {bob_IP, alice_IP,           │
│   charlie_IP}                 │
└───────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Conflict Scenarios

### Scenario 1: Different Users, Same Group

```
Local:  bob → engineering
OIDC:   alice → engineering

group:engineering = {bob, alice}
```

No conflict. Both users are included.

### Scenario 2: Same User in Both Sources

```
Local:  bob → engineering
OIDC:   bob → engineering

group:engineering = {bob}  (counted once)
```

Deduplication by user ID prevents double-counting.

### Scenario 3: Group Exists in Only One Source

```
Local:  bob → local-team     (policy only)
OIDC:   alice → oidc-team    (OIDC only)

group:local-team = {bob}
group:oidc-team  = {alice}
```

Each group resolves independently from its source.

### Scenario 4: Group in Neither Source

```
group:nonexistent = {} (empty set)
```

No users, no nodes, no filter rules. The ACL is a no-op.

### Scenario 5: OIDC Refresh Doesn't Touch Local Groups

```
Before refresh:
  bob (local) + alice (OIDC) in engineering

OIDC refresh removes alice from engineering.

After refresh:
  bob (local) still in engineering
  alice removed from OIDC only
```

The policy's `groups` section is never modified by OIDC refresh.
The `user_oidc_groups` table is never modified by local changes.

---

## Source Isolation

| | Local Groups | OIDC Groups |
|---|---|---|
| **Storage** | Policy `groups` section (in-memory) | `user_oidc_groups` DB table |
| **Modified by OIDC refresh?** | No | Yes |
| **Modified by local changes?** | Yes (policy reload) | No |
| **Auditable separately?** | Yes (read the policy) | Yes (query the DB) |

---

## Code Path

### `Group.resolve()` in `hscontrol/policy/v2/types.go`

```go
func (g *Group) resolve(p *Policy, users types.Users,
    nodes views.Slice[types.NodeView]) (*netipx.IPSet, error) {

    var ips netipx.IPSetBuilder

    // Phase 1: Local groups from policy
    for _, username := range p.Groups[*g] {
        uips, err := username.resolve(nil, users, nodes)
        ips.AddSet(uips)
    }

    // Phase 2: OIDC groups from DB
    if p.oidcGroupResolver != nil {
        groupName := strings.TrimPrefix(string(*g), "group:")
        oidcUsers, err := p.oidcGroupResolver.GetUsersByOIDCGroup(groupName)
        if err == nil && len(oidcUsers) > 0 {
            // Deduplicate
            localUserIDs := make(map[uint]bool)
            for _, u := range p.Groups[*g] {
                if user, err := u.resolveUser(users); err == nil {
                    localUserIDs[user.ID] = true
                }
            }
            for _, oidcUser := range oidcUsers {
                if localUserIDs[oidcUser.ID] {
                    continue
                }
                for _, node := range nodes.All() {
                    if node.User().ID() == oidcUser.ID {
                        node.AppendToIPSet(&ips)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return ips.IPSet(), nil
}
```

### DB Layer in `hscontrol/db/users.go`

```go
// SetUserOIDCGroups replaces all OIDC groups for a user.
func SetUserOIDCGroups(tx *gorm.DB, userID types.UserID,
    groupNames []string) error {
    // Hard delete (Unscoped) to allow re-insertion
    tx.Unscoped().Where("user_id = ?", userID).Delete(&types.UserOIDCGroup{})
    // Insert new groups
    tx.Create(&groups)
}

// GetUsersByOIDCGroup returns all users in a given OIDC group.
func GetUsersByOIDCGroup(tx *gorm.DB, groupName string) ([]types.User, error) {
    return tx.Joins("JOIN user_oidc_groups ON ...").
        Where("group_name = ?", groupName).Find(&users)
}
```

### OIDC Callback in `hscontrol/oidc.go`

```go
// Store OIDC group memberships after login
if err := a.h.state.SetUserOIDCGroups(
    types.UserID(user.ID), []string(claims.Groups)); err != nil {
    log.Error().Err(err).Msg("failed to store OIDC groups")
}
```

---

## Policy Syntax

```json
{
  "groups": {
    "group:local-team": ["bob@headscale.local"]
  },
  "acls": [
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:engineering"],
      "dst": ["group:admins:443"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["group:local-team", "tag:server"],
      "dst": ["*:80"]
    }
  ]
}
```

- `group:engineering` → resolves from OIDC (and local if defined)
- `group:local-team` → resolves from local policy
- `tag:server` → standard Tailscale tag
- `oidcgrp:` → **rejected** at parse time (not Tailscale-compatible)

---

## What `oidcgrp:` Was and Why It Was Removed

The original implementation used `oidcgrp:<name>` as a separate principal type:

```json
// OLD: not Tailscale-compatible
{ "src": ["oidcgrp:engineering"] }
```

This was rejected because:
1. Tailscale uses `group:<name>` as the standard principal
2. Adding `oidcgrp:` creates a non-standard extension
3. Policies would not be portable between Tailscale SaaS and self-hosted Headscale

The new implementation merges OIDC groups into the existing `group:` resolution:

```json
// NEW: Tailscale-compatible
{ "src": ["group:engineering"] }
```

---

## Security Properties

1. **Stale memberships**: Periodic refresh clears old OIDC groups. Fresh groups
   populate on next login.

2. **Privilege removal**: Removing a user from an OIDC group removes their
   authorization after the next refresh.

3. **Source isolation**: OIDC refresh never touches the policy's `groups` section.
   Local changes never touch the `user_oidc_groups` table.

4. **Concurrency**: `PolicyManager` uses `sync.RWMutex`. The `oidcGroupResolver`
   is set once at startup and preserved across policy reloads.

5. **Empty response**: If the OIDC provider returns no groups, only local
   memberships apply. No crash or error.

title: dns: cancel extra-records retry on shutdown
body:
When `dns.extra_records_path` is deleted or atomically replaced, the filewatcher retry can ignore shutdown for up to 15 minutes. This change cancels that retry on `Close` and closes the watcher if setup fails.

## Problem

`NewExtraRecordsManager` starts an `fsnotify` watcher and `Run` re-attaches after `Remove`/`Rename` with `backoff.Retry`. That retry used `context.Background()`, so `Close()` (called from `Serve` shutdown) could not abort it. backoff v5's default budget is 15 minutes.

If the file is still missing after that budget, the old loop continued without `watcher.Add`. A later recreate of the same path was never seen. That is a delayed return of the watch-loss bug fixed in #2298 for editor atomic saves.

Setup errors after `fsnotify.NewWatcher()` also returned without `watcher.Close()`, leaking the watcher FD and its internal goroutine.

## Change

- Cancel the path-exists retry when `closeCh` is closed.
- After a failed retry that is not shutdown, watch the parent directory so a later recreate is observed.
- Close the watcher on every `NewExtraRecordsManager` error path after `NewWatcher` succeeds.

## Validation

- Red: `go test ./hscontrol/dns/ -run TestWaitUntilPathExistsReturnsOnClose` failed in 2s without the cancel (`waitUntilPathExists did not return after Close`).
- Green: `go test -race ./hscontrol/dns/` passes.
- `gofmt` and `golangci-lint run ./hscontrol/dns/` are clean.

title: configtest runs database migrations against the configured DB, not a pure config validator
body:
## What happened

`headscale configtest` is documented as "Run a test of the configuration and exit", but it constructs the full server, which opens the configured database and **runs all pending migrations**. We hit this operationally while staging an upgrade:

1. Production server running X, live sqlite DB at schema X.
2. Ran `configtest` with the Y (newer) binary against the same config/DB to pre-validate the config; it exited 0.
3. Rolled back the server to X for unrelated reasons and X refused to start: schema had been forward-migrated to Y by `configtest` alone. (Migrations are forward-only, so rollback required a DB restore from snapshot.)

## Code path (master @ cbe3030)

- `cmd/headscale/cli/configtest.go`: `RunE` calls `newHeadscaleServerWithConfig()`
- `cmd/headscale/cli/utils.go:89`: same constructor `serve` uses
- `hscontrol/app.go`: `NewHeadscale` -> `state.NewState(cfg)`
- `hscontrol/state/state.go:228`: `hsdb.NewHeadscaleDatabase(cfg)` opens the DB and runs gormigrate with the full migration list

So `configtest` is exactly `serve` minus the listen, including DB mutation. `NewState` also loads all nodes and marks them offline in memory; whether any of that persists depends on the gorm session, but the migrations definitely do.

## Expected

Either:

- `configtest` validates config (and policy/ACL syntax) **without** opening the database, or
- it opens the DB read-only / skips migrations, or
- at minimum the help text warns that it mutates the configured database.

Happy to send a PR if there's agreement on which behaviour is intended. My vote is the first: validate config + policy parsing only, no DB, since that's what the command name and help promise.

title: [Bug] acmeLogger drains the ACME error body, breaking badNonce retries and stopping certificate renewal permanently
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

`acmeLogger.RoundTrip` (added in #2933) reads and closes the response body of every ACME response with status >= 400, and then hands that response back to `golang.org/x/crypto/acme`:

```go
if resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusBadRequest {
	defer resp.Body.Close()

	body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	log.Error().Int("status_code", resp.StatusCode).Str("url", req.URL.String()).Bytes("body", body).Msg("acme request returned error")
}

return resp, nil
```

The acme client parses that body to classify the error. With an empty body, `responseError` (`acme/http.go`) cannot unmarshal the problem document, so `ProblemType` stays empty and `isBadNonce` (`acme/jws.go`) returns false. In `Client.post` (`acme/http.go`) `badNonce` is the only reason a 400 is retried, and it is also the only place that calls `clearNonces`:

```go
switch {
// Check for bad nonce before isRetriable because it may have been returned
// with an unretriable response code such as 400 Bad Request.
case isBadNonce(resErr):
	// Consider any previously stored nonce values to be invalid.
	c.clearNonces()
case !isRetriable(res.StatusCode):
	return nil, resErr
}
```

So a `badNonce` reply now terminates the renewal attempt instead of being retried, and the stale nonce pool is never cleared.

That turns into a permanent deadlock. autocert retries a failed renewal after roughly 30-60 minutes. The 400 response carries a fresh `Replay-Nonce`, which the client stores in its pool; by the time of the next attempt that nonce has expired on the CA side, so the next attempt fails with `badNonce` again. Our server was stuck in that loop for a month:

- 920 `acme request returned error` / `badNonce` log lines, ~32 per day
- exactly one line per attempt, i.e. no retry ever happened
- the certificate expired and every client dropped with `x509: certificate has expired`
- restarting headscale fixed it instantly, because a fresh process starts with an empty nonce pool and fetches a new nonce via `new-nonce`

Log sample, the same line repeating for a month:

```
2026-09-08T08:36:25Z ERR acme request returned error body="{\n  \"type\": \"urn:ietf:params:acme:error:badNonce\",\n  \"detail\": \"JWS has an invalid anti-replay nonce\",\n  \"status\": 400\n}" status_code=400 url=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/new-order
```

The ACME account, DNS, TLS-ALPN-01 reachability and the system clock were all fine — the very same setup issued a new certificate seconds after a restart.

There is some irony here: the middleware was added to make failing renewals debuggable, and it is what makes them permanent.

### Expected Behavior

`acmeLogger` logs the error response and leaves the body readable for the acme client, so `badNonce` is detected, the nonce pool is cleared and the request is retried.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run headscale >= v0.29 with `tls_letsencrypt_hostname` / autocert.
2. Let one ACME request fail with `urn:ietf:params:acme:error:badNonce`.
3. Every following renewal attempt fails the same way until the process is restarted, and the certificate eventually expires.

It also reproduces without a CA: serve a 400 `badNonce` problem document through `acmeLogger` and observe that the response body reaching the acme client is empty, so `acme.Error.ProblemType` is empty instead of `urn:ietf:params:acme:error:badNonce`.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04
- Headscale version: v0.29.2 (code is unchanged in v0.29.3 and in main)
- golang.org/x/crypto: v0.53.0
- Tailscale version: 1.9x
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is running as a systemd service
- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Certificate cache before and after the restart (`/var/lib/headscale/<hostname>`), the ECDSA entry had expired and was reissued within seconds of the restart with no configuration change.

### Contribution

- [x] I can write the fix, PR follows
