title: all: automate the version bumps
body:
`gh-actions-updater.yaml` has failed weekly since `secrets.WORKFLOW_SECRET`
stopped existing — `Input required and not supplied: token`. `update-flake.yml`
was deleted before it because its pull requests got no CI: `GITHUB_TOKEN` does
not trigger `pull_request` workflows.

That leaves four interlocked pins to move by hand:

- `modernc.org/libc` must match what `modernc.org/sqlite` requires.
- `gvisor.dev/gvisor` must match what `tailscale.com` requires.
- Any `go.mod` change needs `go run ./cmd/vendorhash update`.
- `go.mod`'s `go` directive must not outrun the Go nixpkgs ships.

`tools/bump` encodes them and opens one pull request. `workflow_dispatch` only
— no schedule until the manual runs are trusted.

```
go run ./tools/bump plan      # what is stale, changes nothing
go run ./tools/bump verify    # do the pins still agree
```

Before it can run, @juanfont needs a fine-grained token from
https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Resource owner | `juanfont` |
| Repository access | Only select repositories → `juanfont/headscale` |
| Contents | Read and write |
| Pull requests | Read and write |
| Workflows | Read and write |

Then store it:

```
gh secret set WORKFLOW_SECRET --repo juanfont/headscale
```

`Workflows` is what lets it bump the action pins. `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not do —
its pull requests get no CI.

title: [Bug] Bug: Inaccessible routes are being advertised/pushed to clients after update
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

After updating Headscale, I observed a regression in how advertised routes are distributed. If Node A advertises multiple routes or subnets, Node B receives all advertised routes from Node A, even if ACL rules explicitly restrict Node B from accessing specific subnets. In previous versions, Headscale filtered out routes that the client had no permission to reach. While Node B still needs access to Node A itself (or other services on it), receiving unauthorized subnet routes can cause local routing conflicts on Node B.

### Expected Behavior

Inaccessible routes should not be pushed to clients that cannot reach them.

### Steps To Reproduce

1- Set up a Headscale network with Node A and Node B.
2- Configure Node A to advertise a subnet route (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24).
3- Configure ACL rules such that Node B can communicate with Node A directly (or access a specific port/service), but is explicitly denied access to the advertised subnet 192.168.1.0/24.
4- Connect both nodes to Headscale and approve the subnet route on Node A.
5- Inspect the routing table on Node B (tailscale status or ip route).

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: debian 13 trixie
- Headscale version: 0.29.3
- Tailscale version: 1.102.3
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Pushing subnet routes to devices that are explicitly denied access to those subnets via ACL makes no practical sense. It bypasses the expected isolation controls and forces client nodes to accept routing entries for networks they cannot interact with.

In our environment, this change broke system routing and created IP/subnet conflicts on client devices. If this routing behavior was changed intentionally for specific edge cases, it should at least be made configurable via config.yaml (e.g., filter_unauthorized_routes: true) so existing deployments don't suffer from unintended network disruption.

title: cli: distinguish no match from ambiguous match when resolving users
body:
`headscale users destroy` and `headscale users rename` resolve the target with
`resolveSingleUser`, which treated every result count other than one as
"multiple users match query, specify an ID". A name that matches nobody got the
same message, which points the operator in the wrong direction.

An explicit `--identifier 0` had a second problem: the flag default is -1, so 0
passed the "is a flag set" check and was sent to the API as `id=0`, which the
list endpoint treats as "no filter". The CLI then received every user and
failed with the same ambiguous-match error.

This change:

- returns "no user matches query" when the list comes back empty
- keeps "multiple users match query, specify an ID" for two or more matches
  (OIDC users can share a name, see #3429)
- rejects an explicit zero or negative `--identifier` before calling the API

`TestResolveSingleUser` now asserts the specific sentinel error for each case
instead of just "an error", and covers the `--identifier 0` regression.

The destroy prompt also now says that nodes owned by the user must be deleted
or moved first, since that is the precondition the API enforces and the prompt
only mentioned pre-auth keys.

title: db: quote postgres connection parameters
body:
The Postgres DSN was assembled by string concatenation:

    dbString += " password=" + cfg.Postgres.Pass

libpq's keyword/value format splits on whitespace, so a password containing a
space was cut off at the space and the remainder parsed as further parameters.
A value with a single quote or backslash broke parsing in similar ways. The
failure is silent: the connection simply fails to authenticate, or worse, a
password containing `sslmode=disable` turns TLS off.

This moves the DSN into a `postgresDSN` helper that quotes every value with
`pgQuote`, following the libpq rules: wrap in single quotes, escape `\` and `'`
with a backslash. Host, database name, user, password and a raw `ssl` value
such as `verify-full` all go through it. The `ssl` handling is unchanged:
`true` keeps the libpq default, `false` adds `sslmode=disable`, anything else
is passed through as an `sslmode` value.

The startup log line used to print the DSN before the password was appended.
It now logs the DSN built from a copy of the config with the password cleared,
so the redaction no longer depends on statement order.

`TestBuildPostgresDSN` covers the three `ssl` forms, a unix-socket host, an
omitted port and password, and a password containing a space, a quote, a
backslash and an embedded `sslmode=disable`. I also confirmed the quoted output
round-trips through pgx's `pgconn.ParseConfig` with the expected host, port,
database, user and password; that check is not committed to keep pgx an
indirect dependency.

`DestroyPreAuthKey` opens a nested transaction with `tx.Transaction(func(db
*gorm.DB) error { ... })` so that clearing `auth_key_id` on referencing nodes
and deleting the key are applied together. The node update used the inner `db`
handle, but the DELETE used the outer `tx`:

    err := db.Model(&types.Node{}).Where("auth_key_id = ?", id).Update("auth_key_id", nil).Error
    ...
    res := tx.Unscoped().Delete(&types.PreAuthKey{}, id)

Both handles share one connection, so the statements run in the same
transaction and the behaviour is correct today. The code still reads as if the
DELETE sits outside the savepoint, and the mismatch is exactly the kind of
thing a future change to `Transaction` or to the caller would turn into a real
bug. Use the inner handle for both statements.

pre-auth key tests cover the path.

title: Fix PTR/search domain generation for octet-aligned subnets
body:
The current implementation of MagicDNS search domain PTR generation for the tailnet subnet does not correctly cater for octet-aligned subnets (e.g. `172.16.0.0/16`). It currently generates 256 entries on byte aligned subnet masks: `172.16.0.0/16` creates ` [0-255].16.172.in-addr.arpa.`.

While the current implementation is functionally correct in a vacuum, it creates an excessive amount of search domain entries, that at minimum, bust the limits of the `systemd-resolved` stub resolver (`resolved` supports 256 maximum entries, with the tailscale client trying to install 257+ search domains - the 256 PTRs and the MagicDNS domain itself when using an octet-aligned subnet).

This fix outputs a single search domain for all octet-aligned subnet masks (`/8`, `/16`, `/24`), with `172.16.0.0/16`  now outputting a single `16.172.in-addr.arpa.` entry.

This fixes implementation also replaces the `/32` special case workaround.

New tests have been added for both octet-aligned (including the `/32` special case) and -unaligned subnets. The existing test for `172.16.0.0/16` has been corrected for the expected single domain output, but could be removed entirely in lieu of the new tests.

I believe this fix is suitable for backporting to the v0.29.x series.

title: [Feature] provide an official Ubuntu PPA for Headscale
body:
## Summary

Please publish Headscale as an Ubuntu PPA (or another apt repository independent of GitHub Releases). Installing Headscale from `github.com` / GitHub release assets is unreliable when GitHub is intermittently unreachable.

## Problem

Headscale is currently installed from GitHub Releases, for example:

`https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/releases/download/v0.29.3/headscale_0.29.3_linux_amd64.deb`

On a freshly provisioned Ubuntu 22.04 VM (Yandex Cloud), cloud-init bootstrap failed while downloading that package:

```
curl: (28) Failed to connect to github.com port 443 after 130121 ms: Connection timed out
```

`cloud-init status` ended in `error`. Headscale was never installed (`headscale` inactive; no `/var/lib/headscale`).

Automation that must finish unattended (cloud-init / Terraform) cannot depend on GitHub remaining reachable for the whole bootstrap.

## Requested outcome

- An official Ubuntu apt source (PPA or equivalent) that serves Headscale packages without fetching GitHub Releases at install time.
- Documented `add-apt-repository` / `sources.list`.

title: db: guard argon2 verification against corrupt hash parameters
body:
`verifySecret` read `time/memory/threads` straight out of the stored PHC string and passed them to argon2.IDKey unchecked. A row written as `m=0,t=0,p=0` parsed cleanly and then panicked inside `argon2.IDKey`, permanently burning a slot from the argon2Limiter semaphore since the release wasn't deferred; enough corrupt rows would deadlock all OAuth authentication. A row with a very large `m=` could also drive an unbounded allocation.

Validate time, threads and memory against zero and a new `argon2MaxMemory` ceiling before calling `argon2.IDKey`, and release the semaphore slot with defer so a panic can't leak it.

title: mapper, state: send removed peers as their own delta
body:
Tailscale clients only report removed peers to IPN bus watchers when they
apply a map response incrementally, and the Android app (since 1.100) relies
on that alone. Headscale worked removals out inside responses carrying
`DNSConfig`, `SSHPolicy`, `Node` or `Peers` (a deletion merged into a policy
recompute, a policy change hiding peers, a full update, the initial map after
a reconnect), each forcing a full netmap rebuild, so the app kept showing the
peer. Removals now lead in a `PeersRemoved`-only response and `DeleteNode`
emits them as their own change; tailscale/tailscale#15660 fixes the client
from 1.104, so the separate frames are marked compat and
`capver.CanOldCodeBeCleanedUp` flags them once 1.104 is the minimum.

Policy responses also stop carrying `DNSConfig`, which forced a full rebuild
on every policy change; a node gets its DNS config with its own refresh when
its NextDNS nodeAttrs, tags or hostname change.

Updates tailscale/tailscale#15660

title: [Bug] via exit-node steering is nullified by any non-via ACL rule matching the viewer

labels.name: well described ❤️
labels.description: Issues that are well described and researched, making it easier for maintainers.

body:
# Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

# Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

(Closest existing: #3233 and #3408, both closed. This is the inverse of #3408 —
there, via-matching exit nodes were wrongly hidden; here, non-matching ones are
wrongly *shown*. I believe PR #3409 over-corrected.)

---

# Current Behavior

A grant restricting internet access to a specific exit node via a tag steers
traffic correctly, but **does not remove the other exit nodes from the viewer's
netmap**. All exit nodes keep `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` in `AllowedIPs`, so they all
appear in the client's exit-node picker. Selecting a non-permitted one produces a
dead tunnel with no error.

The exclusion is computed correctly and then deleted again. The trigger is the
presence of **any** non-via grant that the viewer matches — regardless of that
grant's destination.

## Root cause

`hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go`, in `ViaRoutesForPeer`
(line 1353 in v0.29.4, line 1421 on `main`):

```go
result.Exclude = slices.DeleteFunc(result.Exclude, dstPrefix.Overlaps)
```

Three things combine:

1. **ACLs are appended to the grant list** as non-via grants:

   ```go
   grants := pm.pol.Grants
   for _, acl := range pm.pol.ACLs {
       grants = append(grants, aclToGrants(acl)...)
   }
   ```

2. **Exit routes enter `Exclude` as `0.0.0.0/0` / `::/0`**, via
   `matchedPrefixes = append(matchedPrefixes, peer.ExitRoutes()...)`.

3. **`netip.Prefix.Overlaps` is symmetric.** `100.64.0.15/32` overlaps
   `0.0.0.0/0`, because the default route contains every address.

So for every non-via grant the viewer matches, every one of its resolved
destination prefixes deletes `0.0.0.0/0` from `Exclude`. A rule as ordinary as
`autogroup:member -> 100.64.0.15:53` is sufficient to disable via steering for
every exit node in the tailnet.

The surrounding comment states the intent:

> Match by overlap so a broader or narrower regular dst still catches the routes
> the via grant added to Include.

That reasoning holds for `Include` / `UsePrimary` on the preceding lines, where
a regular grant legitimately defers to HA primary election. Reusing the same
symmetric overlap for `Exclude` is the defect: for exit nodes the excluded
prefix is the one prefix that overlaps everything.

Because the packet filter is a separate layer, traffic restriction still works —
only the advertised routes are wrong. This makes the bug easy to miss: the
policy looks enforced, but the client offers choices that silently fail.

# Expected Behavior

An exit node that does not carry the grant's `via` tag should not advertise
`0.0.0.0/0` / `::/0` to a viewer whose only route to `autogroup:internet` is
through that grant, and should therefore not appear in that viewer's exit-node
list.

Unrelated ACL rules should not affect this, regardless of their destination.

# Steps To Reproduce

1. Register two exit nodes, both advertising and approved for `0.0.0.0/0` +
   `::/0`. Tag one `tag:exit-a`, the other `tag:exit-b`.
2. Register a user-owned client node for `user1@`.
3. Apply this policy:

   ```jsonc
   {
     "tagOwners": {
       "tag:exit-a": ["user1@"],
       "tag:exit-b": ["user1@"],
     },
     "grants": [
       {
         "src": ["autogroup:member"],
         "dst": ["autogroup:internet"],
         "ip":  ["*"],
         "via": ["tag:exit-a"],
       },
     ],
   }
   ```

4. On the client: `tailscale status --json`. Only the `tag:exit-a` node has
   `0.0.0.0/0` in `AllowedIPs`. **This is correct.**
5. Now add a single, unrelated ACL rule whose source matches the same viewer —
   any destination will do:

   ```jsonc
   "acls": [
     { "action": "accept", "src": ["autogroup:member"], "dst": ["autogroup:self:*"] },
   ],
   ```

6. Reload the policy and re-check `tailscale status --json`. **Both** exit nodes
   now carry `0.0.0.0/0`, and both appear in the picker. Traffic is still
   correctly restricted to `tag:exit-a`.

Step 5 is the whole bug: adding a rule that has nothing to do with exit nodes
disables via steering for all of them.

## Controlled confirmation on a live tailnet

Four approved exit nodes, one tagged `tag:exit-public`. Read from
`tailscale status --json`, not the UI:

| policy | exit nodes with `0.0.0.0/0` in viewer's `AllowedIPs` |
|---|---|
| production (viewer matches 3 ordinary ACL rules) | all four |
| identical, but every ACL source repointed away from the viewer | **only the `tag:exit-public` node** |
| reverted to production | all four again |

To make the viewer match no non-via grant, every ACL source was repointed at a
different user, and the viewer was removed from both groups it belonged to —
including one whose only rule was `group:ha -> <host>:8123`, which triggers the
same wipe.

# Environment

```markdown
- OS: Debian 13 (trixie), kernel 6.12.85
- Headscale version: 0.29.4 (also present on `main`)
- Tailscale version: 1.102.4 (macOS), 1.102.5 (linux); reproduced on iOS too
- Number of nodes: 18, of which 4 are approved exit nodes
- Policy mode: file
- TLS: headscale's built-in Let's Encrypt, no reverse proxy
```

# Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

# Debug information

- Code path: `ViaRoutesForPeer` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go`) ->
  `State.RoutesForPeer` (`hscontrol/state/state.go:1303`) ->
  `MapResponseBuilder.buildTailPeers` (`hscontrol/mapper/builder.go:279`),
  which calls `RoutesForPeer` unconditionally for every peer.
- The existing tests `TestViaRoutesForPeer` and
  `issue_3233_test.go::ViaRoutesForPeer_excludes_exit_for_other_tag` pass,
  because they call `ViaRoutesForPeer` with policies that contain **only**
  grants. Adding one ACL rule matching the viewer should make the latter fail —
  that may be the cheapest regression test for this.

## Suggested fix

Never let a narrower destination evict a default route:

```go
result.Exclude = slices.DeleteFunc(result.Exclude, func(p netip.Prefix) bool {
    if tsaddr.IsExitRoute(p) && !tsaddr.IsExitRoute(dstPrefix) {
        return false
    }
    return dstPrefix.Overlaps(p)
})
```

## On netmap dumps and trace logs

Deliberately not attached. The failure is fully determined by the policy and is
reproducible from the six steps above on any two-exit-node tailnet — a netmap
dump from my deployment would add node keys, tailnet addressing and client
endpoints without adding information about the bug.

The observable is a single field: whether the non-`via` exit node carries
`0.0.0.0/0` in the viewer's `AllowedIPs`. That flips purely on whether an
unrelated ACL rule matching the viewer is present.

Happy to provide netmap dumps, trace logs or the full policy on request.

---

*Disclosure: this report was written with the assistance of an LLM. The source
analysis and the before/after `AllowedIPs` results were verified by hand against
a live 0.29.4 deployment.*

title: [Bug] Serve goroutines are forcefully stopped
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

`Serve` has several `context.Background()`s passed to goroutines, ex: https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/393dd3e2d94e7d999b423d0265b21014a98b6ca0/hscontrol/app.go#L632

That makes it so the other goroutines will get killed while they are doing their work (serve network requests, run scheduled tasks, etc.)

### Expected Behavior

Goroutines started by `Serve` use the same base context. When that context is cancelled, goroutines observe it and stop their in-progress work.

### Steps To Reproduce

I don't have steps, but this kind of problem causes:
- errors on client-side: their network responses are cut midway
- program does not respond to shutdown signals
- if one goroutine errors the program keeps working with unhealthy state
- timing/flaky issues at shutdown

### Environment


title: state: build the peer map once per node write
body:
A tag, user, IP or route write built the peer map twice, first with matchers the policy manager had not yet recompiled; the O(N²) build is the cost behind #3417. Refreshing policy nodes inside the `NodeStore` build makes it one build with current matchers, and auto-approved routes now ride the map request's own write.

Also fixes two policy bugs 0.29 has too: a rejected policy left its filter live in memory, and per-node filters under `autogroup:self` went stale after a user rename.

Updates #3417

### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

A node that advertises exit routes never receives its own updated self node after the routes are approved with `headscale nodes approve-routes`. On the node, `tailscale status --json` keeps `.Self.ExitNodeOption = false` and `.Self.AllowedIPs` without `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`, `tailscale status` does not print "offers exit node", and `tailscale debug netmap` shows `SelfNode.Hostinfo.RoutableIPs = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]` next to `SelfNode.AllowedIPs = ["100.64.0.1/32", "fd7a:115c:a1e0::1/128"]`. Nothing changes over time: the node only learns its approved routes when it opens a new map session (`systemctl restart tailscaled`, `tailscale down && tailscale up`).

Up to v0.29.3, withdrawing and re-advertising the routes on the node (`tailscale set --advertise-exit-node=false && tailscale set --advertise-exit-node`) made headscale send the node its self node, which was a usable workaround. Since v0.29.4 that no longer has any effect: `Self.ExitNodeOption` stays `false` after the toggle too.

With headscale logging at `trace`, both the gRPC approval and each half of the toggle end in `node change processing started node.id=1 reason="policy change"` followed by `update sent` on the node's stream, and the node's self stays unchanged (full log below).

### Expected Behavior

After `headscale nodes approve-routes`, the approved node receives a map response carrying its updated self node, so `Self.AllowedIPs` contains the approved exit routes and `Self.ExitNodeOption` is `true` on its live map session, without restarting tailscaled. Re-advertising the routes should keep refreshing the node's self as it did on v0.29.3.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. headscale v0.29.4, one user, no policy.
2. On a node (tailscale 1.102.4): `tailscale up --login-server https://<headscale> --auth-key <key> --advertise-exit-node`.
3. `headscale nodes approve-routes --identifier <id> --routes 0.0.0.0/0,::/0`.
4. On the node, wait a minute, then `tailscale status --json | jq .Self.ExitNodeOption` → `false`; `tailscale debug netmap | jq '.SelfNode | {AllowedIPs, Hostinfo: {RoutableIPs: .Hostinfo.RoutableIPs}}'` shows the routes announced but absent from `AllowedIPs`.
5. `tailscale set --advertise-exit-node=false && tailscale set --advertise-exit-node`, wait → still `false` (on v0.29.3 this step flips it to `true`).
6. `systemctl restart tailscaled` → `true`.

### Environment

- OS: Debian 13 (headscale container and the tailscale node)
- Headscale version: 0.29.4 (image `headscale/headscale:v0.29.4`); the first part also reproduces on 0.29.3
- Tailscale version: 1.102.4
- Number of nodes: 1 (the exit node itself; no other node needed to observe it)
- Policy: none

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Where it comes from (from the v0.29.4 source)

The mapper only adds the self node to a response when the change's `OriginNode` is the receiving node: `isSelfUpdate := r.OriginNode != 0 && r.OriginNode == nodeID` ([`batcher.go:106`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go#L106)), passed as `includeSelf` to `policyChangeResponse` ([`batcher.go:128`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go#L128), [`mapper.go:353-355`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/mapper/mapper.go#L353-L355)).

1. `State.SetApprovedRoutes` always ends with `if routeChange || !c.IsFull() { c = change.PolicyChange() }` ([`state.go:1053-1055`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L1053-L1055)). `c` is never `IsFull()` there, so the gRPC/CLI approval always fans out a bare `PolicyChange()` with `OriginNode == 0`, and the approved node never gets its self. This part is the same on v0.29.3 and on `main`.
2. Since v0.29.4, `NodeView.HasPolicyChange` also compares `ExitRoutes()` ([`node.go:1233`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/types/node.go#L1233), commit 4411264e, cherry-pick of 905ab92f from #3450, backported in #3467). A node re-advertising its already-approved exit routes therefore makes `PolicyManager.SetNodes` return `true` even when the filter hashes match ([`policy.go:900`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go#L900), the "all hashes match" line in the trace), `updatePolicyManagerNodes` returns `change.PolicyChange()` ([`state.go:2899`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L2899)), and `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` returns it before `buildMapRequestChangeResponse` could produce `change.NodeAdded(id)` with its `OriginNode` ([`state.go:3265-3276`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L3265-L3276)). On v0.29.3 the same request ended in `NodeAdded(id)` and `selfMapResponse`, which is why the toggle used to work.

From the code, peers are not affected: the policy response still sends them the node with its routes. Only the node's own view is stale, and nothing refreshes it while its map session stays up.

#2978 / #2996 fixed the same omission for tags by setting `c.OriginNode = nodeID` in `SetNodeTags` ([`state.go:1018`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/v0.29.4/hscontrol/state/state.go#L1018)). Doing the same for the change returned by `SetApprovedRoutes`, and for the policy change returned from a node's own map request in `UpdateNodeFromMapRequest`, makes the node receive its self node in both cases; I will open a PR. The open draft #3501 rewrites these lines but still returns a bare `PolicyChange()` for an announced route, so it does not change this behaviour.

title: state: send a node its own self after its routes change
body:
- [x] have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) file
- [x] raised a GitHub issue or discussed it on the projects chat beforehand
- [x] added unit tests
- [x] added integration tests
- [ ] updated documentation if needed
- [x] updated CHANGELOG.md

Fixes #3502

### What

A node never received its own updated self node after its routes were approved, so on its live map session `Self.AllowedIPs` stayed without the approved exit routes and `tailscale status` never printed "offers exit node" until tailscaled restarted. Since 0.29.4 the same happens when the node withdraws and re-advertises the routes, which used to be the workaround.

### Why

The mapper only adds the self node when `Change.OriginNode` is the receiving node (`batcher.go` `isSelfUpdate`, `policyChangeResponse(..., includeSelf)`). Two paths lose that origin:

- `State.SetApprovedRoutes` ends with `if routeChange || !c.IsFull() { c = change.PolicyChange() }`, which is always taken, so the gRPC/CLI approval fans out a bare `PolicyChange()`.
- `State.UpdateNodeFromMapRequest` returns the policy change from `updatePolicyManagerNodes` before `buildMapRequestChangeResponse` could produce `change.NodeAdded(id)`. Since 4411264e / 905ab92f (#3450, backported in #3467) `HasPolicyChange` compares `ExitRoutes()`, so a re-advertise now takes that early return.

The fix stamps `OriginNode` on the change in both places, the same way `SetNodeTags` does since #2996. Nothing else changes: the batcher already turns an origin into `policyChangeResponse(includeSelf=true)`, peers keep receiving the same policy response, `Change.Merge` already preserves `OriginNode`.

### Tests

- `hscontrol/state`: `TestMapRequestRouteChangeIsSelfUpdate` asserts `OriginNode` on the change returned by `SetApprovedRoutes` and by three map requests (announce, withdraw, re-announce). Fails on `main` (`OriginNode: 0`), passes with the fix.
- `hscontrol/servertest`: `TestRoutes/advertiser_learns_own_approved_exit_routes` drives two real control clients: the advertiser sees `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` in its own `SelfNode.AllowedIPs` after the approval, loses them after a withdrawal and gets them back after a re-advertise, all on the same session; the observer still sees them on the peer.
- `integration`: `TestSubnetRouterMultiNetworkExitNode` now also asserts `Self.ExitNodeOption` and `Self.AllowedIPs` on the exit node itself after `ApproveRoutes`, before the peer is told to use it.

### Notes

- The open draft #3501 rewrites the same lines; both hunks rebase onto it as one assignment after its `if/else` in `SetApprovedRoutes` and one before its kept `return policyChange`. Happy to rebase whichever lands second.
- The `SetApprovedRoutes` part affects 0.29.x too: a backport to `release-branch/0.29` would be welcome.

`AGENTS.md` says `tools/bump` "opens one pull request a day". It has run
zero times since it merged: the workflow only had `workflow_dispatch`, so
nothing ever started it.

Adds `cron: "0 4 * * *"`. Early enough that the pull request it opens has
its checks finished before anyone looks.

The job guard is unchanged and already handles this — a scheduled run is
not `workflow_dispatch`, so it falls through to
`github.repository == 'juanfont/headscale'`, and GitHub does not run
schedules in forks anyway.

A scheduled run passes no inputs, so it takes the defaults already in the
run step: every area, `gate=full`, no dry run, no force.

title: [Bug] OIDC Client Secret required when using PKCE flow
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

My headscale server is using OIDC via PKCE, similar to this:
```yaml
oidc:
  only_start_if_oidc_is_available: true
  issuer: "https://auth.example.com"
  client_id: "123456789"
  client_secret: "" # Same behaviour when the value is absent
  pkce:
    enabled: true
  ...
```

PKCE just uses a client ID, not a client secret. This worked in previous versions of Headscale that supported PKCE, but v0.29.4 fails to start with this configuration:
```
Error: initializing: loading configuration: oidc.client_secret or oidc.client_secret_path is required when oidc.issuer is set
```

Release notes for v0.29.4 mention
> Harden the OIDC callback: [...] an invalid oidc.issuer or a missing oidc.client_id/oidc.client_secret now fails at startup https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/pull/3334

However it should be a valid configuration to have a missing `oidc.client_secret` when `oidc.pkce.enabled` is true.

Setting the following configuration works around the issue, and login still works because the value isn't used:
```yaml
oidc:
  ...
  client_secret: "unused-put-anything-here"
  ...
```


### Expected Behavior

The server should start with a missing `oidc.client_secret` when `oidc.pkce.enabled` is true

### Is this a support request?

### Current Behavior

Removing given ssh access by deleting the `ssh` key in the ACL policy file does not block subsequent ssh connections.

### Expected Behavior

Removing given ssh access by deleting the `ssh` key in the ACL policy file blocks subsequent ssh connections.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. policy.mod = database
2. have two machines to act as the ssh server and ssh client
3. start with a policy file that does not allow ssh and confirm `tailscale ssh` will not connect
```json
{
  "acls": [],
}
```
4. assign ssh access to a user and confirm `tailscale ssh` connects
```json
{
  "acls": [],
  "ssh": [
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["autogroup:member"],
      "dst": ["autogroup:self"],
      "users": ["root"],
    },
 ],
}
```
5. return the policy to the original version from 3. that does not allow ssh
6. `tailscale ssh` still accepts connections

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: linux
- Headscale version: v0.29.4
- Tailscale version: v1.102.4
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

The root cause seems to be this early return nil, nil.
https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/99cbba7aff2bd78c62486212f6968c0cca62870c/hscontrol/policy/v2/filter.go#L261-L263
A nil *tailcfg.SSHPolicy means for callers no update is needed.

I think the fix is to make it `return &tailcfg.SSHPolicy{}, nil`. I can submit a pr with the fix and a test for it. Let me know if it should be fixed a different way.

title: [Bug] 0.29: ViaRoutesForPeer re-resolves the whole policy for every viewer/peer pair; netmap never delivered to nodes with ~950 peers

labels.name: well described ❤️
labels.description: Issues that are well described and researched, making it easier for maintainers.

body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

After upgrading 0.26.1 → 0.27.1 → 0.28.0 → 0.29.4 (one step at a time), our two HA subnet routers never received a netmap again. We had to roll back to 0.26.1 by restoring the database. The policy uses **no `via` grant, no `grants` at all, and no `autogroup:self`** — only `groups`, `hosts`, `tagOwners` and `acls`.

**Tailnet size**

- 1026 nodes (100–180 online), 685 users, PostgreSQL
- 2 HA subnet routers advertising ~60 routes each. They have **946 peers each**; the average node has 5.9 peers (`/debug/nodestore`)
- Policy: 50 `acls` rules, 341 destinations in total, 54 groups listing 2056 usernames

**Symptoms on 0.29.4**

- headscale CPU: 4–9 cores (0.2–0.6 on 0.26.1, ~1.3 on 0.27.1 and 0.28.0)
- Almost every `/machine/map` request ends with `bytes=0`
- Routers register fine (`machineAuthorized=true`), then never reach `Running`
- Clients log `PollNetMap: ... unexpected EOF` every 60 s (reverse proxy read timeout). With the proxy timeout raised to 3600 s, they log `control: map response long-poll timed out!` every 120 s instead, and the request is queued again
- CLI calls exceed the 5 s deadline (`DeadlineExceeded`); `headscale nodes rename` took ~15 s

**Reproduced in isolation**: a local headscale 0.29.4 on a copy of the database, no reverse proxy, **a single client** registered as the router's user. One core is busy at 100 %, one map was eventually delivered after **96 s** (`bytes=366760 elapsed=96213`), the next request ended with `bytes=0` after 157 s because the client gave up at 120 s.

**On 0.26.1, same data, same router**: the netmap arrives within 1 second of registration, and a 30 s CPU profile shows 1.5 s of CPU in total.

**CPU profile on 0.29.4 (production, 6 s, 26 s of samples)** — 89 % of the time is in:

```
mapper.(*Batcher).worker
 mapper.generateMapResponse
  mapper.(*MapResponseBuilder).buildTailPeers
   types.NodeView.TailNode
    state.(*State).RoutesForPeer
     policy/v2.(*PolicyManager).ViaRoutesForPeer     23.27s  89.36%
      policy/v2.(*Group).Resolve                     23.11s  88.75%
       policy/v2.(*Username).resolve                 21.75s  83.53%
        policy/v2.(*Username).resolveUser            14.40s  55.30%
```

**Goroutine dump at the same time**: 106 goroutines waiting in `mapper.(*Batcher).MapResponseFromChange` (called from `AddNode`), 4 workers computing inside `ViaRoutesForPeer`, 2–3 workers waiting on a mutex in `Batcher.worker`.

**What we think happens (reading v0.29.4)**

Three factors multiply:

1. `buildTailPeers` (`hscontrol/mapper/builder.go`) calls `State.RoutesForPeer` → `ViaRoutesForPeer` for **every peer**, including peers that advertise no route at all (only 3 of our 1026 nodes have routes).
2. `ViaRoutesForPeer` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go`) converts every ACL to grants and resolves the sources and destinations of **all** of them before checking `len(grant.Via) == 0`. With no `via` grant in the policy, the result is always empty, so all that work is discarded. The function comment already says: "Hot callers should memoise by (policy-hash, viewer-id) rather than invoking this per-pair."
3. `aclToGrants` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/types.go`) emits **one grant per destination**, each carrying the full source list. Our 50 ACL rules become 341 grants, so a rule with 67 destinations has its sources resolved 67 times.

Each `Username.resolve` walks all users and then all nodes, with no cache, and a username matching no user also builds a formatted error.

For our policy this gives 17 691 username resolutions per (viewer, peer) pair, i.e. about 30 million comparisons per pair and about 28.6 billion for one map with 946 peers, which matches the ~96 s we measured.

Related: #3346 (same symptoms after 0.28 → 0.29.1, on a ~200 device tailnet).


### Expected Behavior

Netmap generation time on 0.29 should stay in the same order of magnitude as on 0.26 for a policy that does not use `via`.

Possible fixes, from cheapest to most complete:

1. In `ViaRoutesForPeer`, return early when no grant in the policy has a `via` tag (ACL-derived grants never have one). This alone removes the cost for every policy without `via`.
2. In `RoutesForPeer` / `buildTailPeers`, skip the via computation for peers that advertise no subnet or exit route.
3. Resolve grant sources and destinations once per policy change (or memoise per policy hash and viewer), instead of once per (viewer, peer) pair.
4. When converting ACLs with `aclToGrants` for this purpose, keep one grant per rule instead of one per destination.

We are happy to test a patch on a copy of our database.


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Use a tailnet with about 1000 nodes and several hundred users, and a policy made of `acls` rules only, with large groups as sources and many destinations per rule (ours: 50 rules, 341 destinations, 54 groups, 2056 usernames). No `grants`, no `via`.
2. Make sure at least one node can see most of the tailnet as peers (in our case a subnet router reachable by everyone: 946 peers).
3. Run headscale 0.29.4 and connect that node.
4. Watch `/machine/map` for that node: the first map takes about 96 s on an otherwise idle server with a single client, and is never delivered when other clients are connected. CPU stays at one full core per busy worker.

Workaround we are evaluating (computed, not yet fully measured): rewriting the `acls` rules as native `grants` with all destinations in one grant (`"ip": ["*"]`) brings the number of source resolutions per pair from 341 down to 52, and removing usernames that match no user brings username resolutions from 17 691 down to 1 025. The compiled filter (`/debug/filter`) is byte-for-byte identical to the one produced by the original `acls` policy.


### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Kubernetes (GKE), official container image
- Headscale version: 0.29.4 (also went through 0.27.1 and 0.28.0; rolled back to 0.26.1)
- Tailscale version: 1.84.2 and 1.102.5 on the subnet routers (containerboot), 1.80 to 1.102 on clients
- Database: PostgreSQL 17
- Policy mode: database
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

We cannot share the database, the policy or client netmaps as they are: they contain real user and customer names. We can produce an anonymised policy with the same shape and the same counts if that helps, and we can test a patch on a copy of the database.

**Policy shape** (mode `database`)

| Section | Count |
|---|---|
| `acls` rules | 50, all `accept`, none with `proto` |
| destinations | 341 in total (335 with port `*`), mostly `hosts` aliases, 34 tags |
| sources | 55 groups, 16 tags, 7 usernames |
| `groups` | 54, listing 2056 usernames (1585 distinct), 1189 of which match no user |
| `hosts` | 65 |
| `tagOwners` | 22 |
| `grants`, `ssh`, `autoApprovers`, `autogroup:*`, `via` | none |

`headscale policy check` accepts this policy on 0.27.1, 0.28.0 and 0.29.4.

**Headscale configuration** (environment variables, secrets and URLs removed)

```
HEADSCALE_POLICY_MODE=database
HEADSCALE_DATABASE_TYPE=postgres
HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V4=100.64.0.0/10
HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V6=fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48
HEADSCALE_DNS_MAGIC_DNS=true
HEADSCALE_DERP_URLS=https://controlplane.tailscale.com/derpmap/default
HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_ENABLED=false
HEADSCALE_LOG_LEVEL=info
oidc: enabled, email_verified_required: false
tuning: defaults (we also tried node_store_batch_size=1000, node_store_batch_timeout=5000ms, batch_change_delay=10s, batcher_workers=4, without restoring service)
```

**Resource usage and timings by version** (same tailnet, same evening, Prometheus)

| | 0.26.1 | 0.27.1 | 0.28.0 | 0.29.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU, average (cores) | 0.33 | 1.24 | 1.37 | 3.52 |
| CPU, max (cores) | 1.03 | 1.33 | 1.41 | 9.47 |
| `headscale_nodestore_peers_calculation_duration_seconds`, average | n/a | 9.4 s | 7.6 s | 13.0 s |
| subnet routers available | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| first netmap for a router with 946 peers | ≤ 1 s | not measured | not measured | never within 120 s |

**Router log on 0.29.4** (Tailscale 1.102.5, `TS_BOOT_TIMEOUT=4m`, reverse proxy timeout raised to 3600 s)

```
19:00:54 control: RegisterReq: got response; nodeKeyExpired=false, machineAuthorized=true; authURL=false
19:00:54 health(warnable=login-state): ok
19:02:54 control: map response long-poll timed out!
19:02:54 Received error: PollNetMap: Post "https://<server>/machine/map": context canceled
```

**Headscale log on 0.29.4** (isolated reproduction, single client)

```

INF http request bytes=0 elapsed=157059.834707 method=POST path=/machine/map proto=HTTP/2.0 status=200
ERR cannot write update to client error="http2: stream closed" component=poll
```

**Goroutine dump on 0.29.4** (production, `/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1`, 370 goroutines)

```

  3  policy/v2.(*Username).resolveUser < (*Username).resolve < (*Group).resolve < (*PolicyManager).ViaRoutesForPeer < (*State).RoutesForPeer
```

title: [Bug] Grants with via for exit nodes works differently for a group and for a user/autogroup
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

The grants with **via** for exit nodes works differently for a group and for a user.

I crete exit node with tag "tag:exitnode". And I created a user group called develop.
```
"group:develop": [
            "develop1@",
            "develop2@",
],
```

When I create a rule
```
      { // access users use exit-node
           "src": [
                "group:develop",
           ],
           "dst": [
                "autogroup:internet"
           ],
           "via": ["tag:exitnode"],
           "ip": ["*"]
      }
```
Users in the group do not receive the list of exit nodes.

But when I specify a user in a grant or "autogroup:member"
```
      { // access users use exit-node
           "src": [
                "develop1@",
           ],
           "dst": [
                "autogroup:internet"
           ],
           "via": ["tag:exitnode"],
           "ip": ["*"]
      }
```
The user begins to see a list of exit nodes with a tag  "tag:exitnode".

### Expected Behavior

A user belonging to a group specified in the grant, and a user explicitly specified in the grant —both must receive the list of exit nodes.

1. greate group with user
```
"group:develop": [
            "develop1@",
            "develop2@",
],
```
2. greate gratn with exit nodes
```
      { // access users use exit-node
           "src": [
                "group:develop",
           ],
           "dst": [
                "autogroup:internet"
           ],
           "via": ["tag:exitnode"],
           "ip": ["*"]
      }
```
3. Log in as the user develop1@ and check the list of exit nodes. The list will be empty.
4. 4.  Change src of  gratn, specify the user or autogroup:member.
```
      { // access users use exit-node
           "src": [
                "develop1@",
           ],
           "dst": [
                "autogroup:internet"
           ],
           "via": ["tag:exitnode"],
           "ip": ["*"]
      }
```

```markdown
- Number of nodes: 4, of which 2 are approved exit nodes
```
